At a time when Nigerians are grappling with unprecedented economic hardship, insecurity and declining living standards, opposition leaders have a responsibility to put the national interest above personal ambitions,” Shaibu told Vanguard.

He said the objectives outlined by the G100 were broadly consistent with Atiku’s longstanding advocacy for opposition cooperation and coalition-building.

“Regarding the August 18 summit, His Excellency is favourably disposed to any sincere engagement that advances opposition unity. His attendance will, however, depend on his schedule and the final arrangements communicated by the organisers,” he said, adding that what mattered most was that Atiku remained committed to working with other opposition leaders towards giving Nigerians a strong, united and credible alternative in 2027.

Nothing wrong with like-minded political leaders uniting – Makinde

Also, Chief Bolaji Ayorinde, SAN, Chairman, Oyo State Advisory Council, said Makinde was disposed to the summit.

He said: “Let me make it clear that there is nothing strange, unlawful or undemocratic about like-minded political leaders coming together to discuss the future of our country and the direction of our democracy.

“If political leaders and stakeholders are meeting to explore the possibility of forming a united political front ahead of 2027, such an initiative should be welcomed as a legitimate exercise in democratic consultation. Nigeria belongs to all of us, and nobody should suggest that political actors must remain permanently divided simply because they have different views about the direction the country should take.

Governor Seyi Makinde is a statesman who understands the importance of dialogue, consultation and building bridges across political divides. He has consistently demonstrated that politics should ultimately be about the welfare of the people and the future of the nation.

Therefore, if discussions are taking place among political leaders to build a broader coalition or united front around a shared vision for Nigeria, I see nothing wrong with that. Democracy thrives on dialogue, negotiations, alliances and the freedom of citizens and political leaders to organise around issues and principles they believe in.

We should not be afraid of political realignment. Indeed, at a time when Nigerians are asking serious questions about the direction of the country, it is only natural for responsible political leaders to consult, exchange ideas and consider alternatives.

What is important is that any such political engagement must be driven by the national interest, democratic principles and the desire to provide Nigerians with credible leadership. It should not be reduced to personal ambition or sectional interest.”

World.title: Why we planned  coup against Tinubu —Col Ma’aji
World.content:
By Kingsley Omonobi

ABUJA — A Nigerian Army Colonel, Mohammed Ma’aji, accused of involvement in an alleged plot to overthrow the government of President Bola Tinubu, has said his actions were driven by patriotism and frustration over what he described as worsening conditions in the country.

His explanations were contained in fresh court records which provided new details about how investigators said a group of military officers and civilians allegedly developed, suspended and later revived a plan to overthrow President Tinubu’s administration.

Defence Headquarters yesterday, said it would not react to the development since the case is still in court.

Director of Defence Information, DDI, Major-General Samaila Uba, said reacting will amount to subjudice.

Colonel Ma’aji said his actions were driven by patriotism and frustration over what he described as worsening conditions in the country.

While apologising for his involvement in the alleged plot and appealing to the authorities for leniency, he insisted that his motive was not personal ambition but a desire for a better Nigeria.

He said the plan emerged from concerns among some military personnel over poor governance, insecurity, inadequate welfare and declining living standards.

According to him, the situation had become so troubling that he feared the country was heading towards collapse.

Ma’aji said: “What has happened has a very long history, and it is driven by patriotism and I love the job and country.

“Every time I look at how I’m struggling to raise five children with my meagre salary, I get worried. Looking at every aspect of life in Nigeria, there is no hope for the common man, and we are left to defend ourselves.

“This has nothing to do with any ambition or personal goals. It is purely out of the desire for a prosperous country that works for everyone.”

He alleged that military personnel were particularly affected by inadequate welfare, citing the condition of soldiers wounded in combat and the challenges facing serving personnel and their families.

The colonel said the movement was still at a stage of mobilisation and discussions when security authorities intervened, adding that no specific date had been agreed for any action.

He also denied that there were foreign collaborators, while explaining that various individuals became involved at different stages of the discussions.

Ma’aji said some of those approached expressed concerns about the state of the country, while others withdrew or failed to provide the resources they had initially promised.

He further said the alleged plot was fuelled by what he described as frustrations over his failure to secure promotion to the rank of brigadier-general on two occasions.

According to him, some of his colleagues had encouraged him to revive the movement after the second setback.

The colonel, who said the initial planning started during the administration of Muhammadu Buhari, however, said his experience, following his arrest, had changed his perspective and made him realise that there were alternative ways of expressing concerns within the military.

“If God willing, the authority is kind enough to pardon us, we will never contemplate this course of action again in the future,” he said.

Ma’aji called for the establishment of a formal channel through which military personnel could communicate their concerns directly to the Chief of Army Staff without fear of victimisation.

He also recommended improved remuneration and welfare packages for members of the Armed Forces, including better healthcare, housing, pension and family support.

The colonel called for an improvement in the military’s casualty management system, saying the treatment of wounded soldiers could affect the morale of personnel still serving in operational areas.

He also criticised what he described as godfatherism and perceived inequality in military postings and career progression, arguing that some officers had spent years on operations while others had little or no operational exposure.

On the wider Nigerian society, Ma’aji expressed concern over the cost of living, education, corruption and the impact of fuel subsidy removal on ordinary citizens.

He urged government to invest resources saved from subsidy reforms in programmes capable of reducing hardship, including mass transportation and other social infrastructure.

He equally called for stronger action against corruption, saying perceived impunity among public officials could affect the morale and confidence of security personnel.

On the alleged coup plot itself, Ma’aji said the movement was never intended to destabilise the country, insisting that it was motivated by what he described as love for Nigeria.

He said: “Everything we planned was borne out of patriotism, love of country, and the desire to have a prosperous Nigeria that we all can be proud of.”

The colonel appealed to the authorities to consider the circumstances that led to the alleged plot and pardon those involved, describing them as first offenders.

“We are pleading for a pardon and a chance to amend our ways. Many of the officers have participated in some operations in the North-East. I am happy nobody has been hurt,” he said.

Approach to expressing grievances

Ma’aji said his detention had been “challenging and revealing”, adding that it had given him an opportunity to reconsider his approach to expressing grievances.

He maintained that he and others involved had no other country to call their own and urged the authorities to consider their contributions to national security alongside the allegations against them.

He stated further: ‘’To prevent a recurrence of incidents such as this, I would advise the authority as follows

‘’Poor remuneration: The salary of Nigerian Armed Forces personnel is too low, considering the current economic realities and inflation.

‘’Welfare: For instance, we are an army at war; our handling of casualties is paramount to how the rest working will be willing to continue and lay their lives for the country. There is also a need for robust welfare packages for all the members of the Armed Forces. There is also a need for serving personnel’s family welfare packages to be introduced. The COAS Loan Programme should be expanded and sustained.

‘’The AF NHIS package needs to be reviewed to include more critical health challenges rather than just malaria and typhoid. There is a need for a sustainable housing programme for the armed forces rather than isolated and disjointed packages.

‘’The issue of the Obasanjo car loan scheme needs to come back. I think the AFN needs a whole department dedicated to personnel welfare. I could elaborate on this if given the opportunity.

‘’Godfatherism: A system where you can hardly get anything without someone calling in on your behalf. There are officers who have been eight, nine years straight on operations. While we still have some officers who haven’t been to the North-East and will never be there.

‘’Pension upgrade: Col Adamu told me that his pension cannot buy his BP drugs. I feel sad when I saw CDS ordering ex-servicemen to be dispersed from their protest ground for improved pensions. We should remember that we shall all retire. Our ex-servicemen deserve better treatment. Charity begins at home; that is why I am starting from the armed forces.

‘’Removal of fuel subsidy: The government should have phased the removal and not the sudden removal, and the policy is anti-human. The primary purpose of government, as provided by the Constitution, is the welfare and security of the people… we have rather created more stealing avenues because governors now have more funds to steal.

‘’An average Nigerian is not asking for too much, just a bare minimum of being able to move from point A to B and also afford three square meals, good health, and the education of their children. The federal government should invest the subsidy money in a practical project that can reduce human suffering. The issue of Urban Mass Transit that started during the military regime should be revisited.

‘’Corruption: This must be given clear and serious attention because it is the mother of all crimes. Our education is in shambles. Those of us here in Abuja, how much do we pay for school fees, and how many officers/soldiers can afford school fees with their salaries?

‘’Budget padding: After padding a budget and awarding costs, they’re still not implemented. For example, you put one thousand naira for a water of 100 naira and still do not buy the water.

‘’These are people who got almost everything free, including education when growing up, but there is no free education anywhere today in Nigeria. They all turned their backs against the country. As a service personnel, how much of salary can you save that would buy you a house to live in ?

‘’Is it after using all your youthful years that you will start looking for money to survive after retirement?

‘’Some officers have served for over 15 years, and even a plot of land they don’t have. The policy of car loans was swept under the carpet. What happened to all these policies? An average officer or soldier is barely surviving, despite the huge sacrifices they are making on a daily basis to keep the country safe and secured. He concluded by asking for an opportunity to meet with the relevant authorities, apologise and commit themselves to pursuing lawful and peaceful means of addressing grievances.

World.title: Troops ambush Lakurawa terrorists in Kebbi, recover items
World.content:
Some recovered items

By Haruna Aliyu, Birnin Kebbi

Troops of Sector 2 Operation FANSAN YAMMA deployed for counter terrorism and anti-banditry operations in Kebbi State have said that they ambushed Lakurawa Terrorist Group (LTG) on transit to wreak havoc in Dandi Local Government Area of Kebbi State.

According to the Acting Director of Army Public Relations, Lieutenant Colonel Olayinka Osoba, the troops, acting on credible intelligence on the movement of Lakurawa terrorists who were on transit, swiftly mobilised and laid a tactical ambush for the terrorists.

The troops intercepted the terrorists at a known crossing point near Uguwan Hassan village.

He added that after making some contacts, the troops engaged the terrorists with superior firepower overwhelmed by the troops’ tactical response, the militants were forced to abandon their mission and retreat in disarray.

Osoba explained that during the encounter, troops recovered some items utilised by the terrorists for logistics and communication, including two motorcycles, mobile phones, T&T communication radios and one Nigerien ID Card belonging to one of the fleeing terrorists from Tilbiri Region of Niger Republic.

“The troops are currently dominating the general area with aggressive patrols and are in active pursuit of the fleeing terrorists to ensure the continued safety and security of the local populace,” he added.

The recent ambush is the latest in a series of counter terrorism gains of the military as they intensify crackdown on armed groups to liberate the northwest.

World.title: 14.5m children registered as Nigeria pushes for legal identity for every child
World.content:
… 6,000 wards now offer digital birth registration — NPC

… FG links birth registration with health, identity systems

By Chioma Obinna

As Nigeria joined other African countries to mark the 2026 Africa Civil Registration and Vital Statistics, CRVS, over 14.5 million Nigerian children have been registered under the country’s intensified birth registration drive even as the Federal Government moves to ensure that every child born in the country has a legal identity.



The National Population Commission, NPC, disclosed that digital birth registration services are now available in more than 6,000 of the country’s 8,809 wards, with registration increasingly linked to health facilities and community outreach programmes.



The 2026 commemoration, which marks the beginning of the new CRVS decade, 2026–2036, is focused on consolidating gains made under the African Programme on Accelerated Improvement of Civil Registration and Vital Statistics, APAI-CRVS, through integration, decentralisation and digitalisation.



The NPC Chairman, Dr Aminu Yusuf, said the commission’s priority was to ensure that no child was excluded from legal recognition because of where he or she was born.



He said: “Every registered birth strengthens the foundation for child protection and national development.



“Our priority is to ensure that every child, regardless of where they are born, is counted, protected and recognised before the law.”



Birth registration, stakeholders said, remains the first formal recognition of a child by the state and provides proof of identity required to access essential services, including healthcare, education and social protection.



It also provides governments with vital demographic data for planning and delivery of public services.

Nigeria’s CRVS system is being strengthened through collaboration among the NPC, National Identity Management Commission, NIMC, Association of Local Governments of Nigeria, ALGON, development partners and communities.



In states including Bayelsa, Gombe, Jigawa, Taraba, Kebbi, Niger and Zamfara, birth registration is increasingly being integrated with health facilities and community-based services to enable parents to register children closer to the point of birth.



Speaking, the Director-General of NIMC, Engr. Abisoye Coker-Odusote, said digital integration would make identity management more seamless from birth to adulthood.



According to Coker-Odusote, “integrated digital identity systems create a seamless pathway for individuals from birth through adulthood, while improving access to services and strengthening governance.”



UNICEF Representative in Nigeria, Wafaa Saeed Abdelatef, said birth registration should not be viewed merely as the issuance of a certificate but as a gateway to a child’s rights.



She said: “Birth registration is far more than a certificate. It is a gateway to protection, services, and opportunity.”



Abdelatef said UNICEF would continue to support the Nigerian government and other partners to strengthen integrated, decentralised and digitalised registration systems.



“As Africa enters a new decade of CRVS systems strengthening, Nigeria remains committed to expanding access to birth registration, improving vital statistics, and ensuring that every child has a legal identity from birth,” she added.



Also, ALGON National President, Hon. Bello Lawal, stressed the importance of decentralising registration services, particularly for children in rural and underserved communities.



He said: “Decentralisation is essential to ensuring that children in remote and underserved communities are not left behind.



“Bringing services closer to families increases access and encourages timely registration.”



Chairman of the House Committee on the National Population Commission, Hon. Okunjimi John Odimayo, said sustained political commitment was critical to building an effective CRVS system.



He noted that strong civil registration and vital statistics systems would support better planning, improved service delivery and stronger development outcomes.



Stakeholders also warned that millions of children across Africa remain without legal identity.



Current estimates indicate that only about half of children under five in sub-Saharan Africa are registered at birth, leaving the region with the largest share of unregistered children globally.

World.title: Nottingham Forest owner sues Crystal Palace over gun banner
World.content:
Marinakis

Nottingham Forest owner Evangelos Marinakis is suing Crystal Palace over a banner unfurled by the London club’s fans depicting him holding a gun to midfielder Morgan Gibbs-White’s head, according to reports on Monday.

Marinakis’ legal team lodged the defamation claim against Palace and “persons unknown” at the High Court in London on Monday, nearly a year on from the banner being displayed during the 1-1 Premier League clash between the two clubs at Selhurst Park.

Alongside the image, the banner read: “Mr Marinakis is not involved in blackmail, match-fixing, drug trafficking or corruption.”

The Greek shipping and media magnate has consistently denied any wrongdoing in relation to such allegations.

In November 2025, the Football Association charged Palace with failing to ensure that supporters did not behave in an improper, offensive, abusive or provocative way and later fined the club £50,000 ($67,000).

The game on August 24 last year took place amid heightened tensions after Forest had taken Palace’s place in the Europa League after the south London club were relegated to the Conference League for breaking UEFA’s multi-club ownership rules.

Marinakis, a 59-year-old Greek businessman, also owns Olympiacos in Greece and Rio Ave in Portugal.

AFP

World.title: NUPRC: Dangote Got 98% of Crude Offered to Local Refineries in Q2
World.content:
Performance rose 97.4% in 3 months

•Supply exceeded allocation, 69.3m barrels offered against 55.1 million

•Supply exceeded allocation, 69.3m barrels offered against 55.1 million Upstream data shows 15.6m barrels unutilised

PENGASSAN: NNPC’s refineries shut down over losses, not non-functionality

Says proposed equity partnership with Chinese firm on right track

Osifo pledges PENGASSAN’s support for Dangote Refinery’s expansion

Emmanuel Addeh in Abuja and Peter Uzoho, Sunday Ehigiator in Lagos

The Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission (NUPRC) has reported a significant improvement in the implementation of the Domestic Crude Supply Obligation (DCSO), with local refiners receiving 53.7 million barrels of crude oil and condensate in the second quarter of 2026, representing a 97.4 per cent performance rate.



According to data released by the Commission yesterday, the Dangote Refinery accounted for the overwhelming majority of the crude supplied to domestic refiners during the quarter.



The NUPRC said the refinery required 63 million barrels during Q2, while producers offered it 68.1 million barrels. The volume represented about 98 per cent of the total 69.3 million barrels offered to all domestic refiners during the quarter.



However, the Dangote refinery accepted 52.6 million barrels, about 77 per cent of the crude offered to it and 10.4 million barrels below its stated requirement.



Its intake also represented about 98 per cent of the 53.7 million barrels eventually supplied to local refiners during the period.



The figures showed that producers were allocated 55.1 million barrels between April and June but offered 69.3 million barrels, exceeding their allocation by 14.2 million barrels, or 25.8 per cent.



Actual supplies, however, stood at 53.7 million barrels, leaving about 15.6 million barrels of the volumes offered unutilised. Supplies were also about 1.4 million barrels below the total volume allocated by the NUPRC.



The DCSO is being enforced by the NUPRC under Section 109 of the Petroleum Industry Act (PIA), which requires oil producers to make crude available to domestic refineries.



According to the Commission, the framework is administered through monthly consultations involving crude oil producers and licensed domestic refineries, after which producers are allocated specific volumes of crude oil and condensate to offer to local refiners.



However, the eventual transactions operate under the PIA’s “willing buyer, willing seller” principle, meaning that volumes offered by producers do not necessarily translate into equivalent quantities purchased and received by refiners.



The quarterly figures also showed significant variations in performance across the three months.



In April, producers were allocated 18.13 million barrels but offered 19.31 million barrels to local refiners. Actual supplies reached 20.88 million barrels, representing 114.9 per cent performance against their allocation.



In May, 18.78 million barrels were allocated and 23.19 million barrels offered, but only 14.23 million barrels were supplied, representing 75.8 per cent compliance. This resulted in a shortfall of about 4.55 million barrels against the month’s allocation.



Performance recovered in June, when producers were allocated 18.17 million barrels and offered 26.84 million barrels to refiners. Actual supplies stood at 18.61 million barrels, representing 102.4 per cent performance.



The monthly data showed that producers consistently offered more crude than their allocated volumes, but actual deliveries were influenced by the quantities refiners were willing or able to take under the commercial arrangements.



The NUPRC said the improvement in DCSO performance coincided with an increase in local oil production and the signing of long-term crude supply agreements supported by bankable Sales and Purchase Agreements (SPAs) between producers and domestic refiners.



The development is significant for Nigeria’s refining ambitions as the country seeks to reduce its dependence on imported petroleum products by ensuring that domestic refineries have adequate crude feedstock.



The Commission said the Q2 results demonstrated that the DCSO was “actively administered and enforced”, adding that it remained committed to sustaining the recent gains.



It said it would continue leveraging the PIA framework to sustain improvements in crude oil production while enforcing the DCSO as part of efforts to achieve the Federal Government’s objective of energy sufficiency.



Meanwhile, Trade Union Congress (TUC) President, Festus Osifo, has disclosed that Nigeria’s public refineries were shut down primarily because they were operating at a financial loss, rather than non-functionality.



Osifo, who is the outgoing President of the Petroleum and Natural Gas Senior Staff Association of Nigeria (PENGASSAN), made the disclosure yesterday, during a luncheon with members of Labour Writers Association of Nigeria (LAWAN).



He explained that although the Port Harcourt and Warri refineries had resumed some level of operations following rehabilitation, the management of the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited (NNPC) subsequently discovered that the value of petroleum products being produced did not justify the cost of crude being processed.



“So, the refineries were actually shut down, not that they were not functioning. Most of the old Port Harcourt Refinery, and even the Warri Refinery, were actually shut down because they were losing money,” Osifo said.



He said the refineries had suffered years of neglect, despite repeated government announcements and approvals for rehabilitation.

According to him, before 2021, there had been little or no meaningful rehabilitation of the facilities for about 15 years, despite several approvals by the Federal Executive Council (FEC).



He likened the situation to road projects that were awarded by the government but remained unexecuted because they were not adequately funded.

“There have been some erroneous impressions over the years that every time they carry out turnaround maintenance and rehabilitation in those refineries. If you interview somebody or people that have worked in Port Harcourt, Kaduna and Warri refinery 15 years before 2021, they will all tell you that they have never seen any rehabilitation or any turnaround maintenance compared to what they’ve seen from 2021,” he stated.



Osifo said significant rehabilitation work subsequently commenced in 2021, particularly at the Port Harcourt Refinery, while work was also carried out at the Warri and Kaduna facilities.



He explained that the Port Harcourt rehabilitation was comprehensive, while the Warri project was more of a quick fix because the level of degradation at the two facilities differed.



According to him, during the rehabilitation of the Port Harcourt Refinery, between 90 and 95 per cent of PENGASSAN members working at the facility were transferred to other Strategic Business Units (SBUs) of NNPCL.



He said the old Port Harcourt Refinery, built in 1965, was eventually restored to operation, while work continued on the new refinery.

Osifo explained that the old refinery could produce Automotive Gas Oil (AGO), Dual Purpose Kerosene (DPK) and aviation fuel, but could not produce Premium Motor Spirit (PMS) to the required modern specification.



He said the old facility was therefore initially feeding products into the new refinery, which was designed to meet current specifications and produce the required petrol.



However, he said the process was later altered because a critical component needed for the completion of the new refinery was expected to take about three and a half years to arrive.



The TUC president said the new management of NNPC subsequently examined the economics of the refinery using the concept of material balance in chemical engineering.



He explained that the cost of crude being fed into the refinery was not being matched by the value of the products being obtained.

According to him, the decision to shut down the facilities was therefore aimed at preventing further losses and reassessing how the refineries could operate profitably.



Osifo argued that the proposed agreement between NNPC and a Chinese company could provide a more sustainable ownership and operational structure for the refineries.



He said PENGASSAN had examined the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between NNPC and the Chinese company and had held discussions with the Group Chief Executive Officer of NNPC on the proposed arrangement. “We think it’s actually in the right direction,” he said.



He disclosed that PENGASSAN had consistently advocated a model similar to the ownership structure of Nigeria LNG Limited (NLNG), where the government retains a minority stake while private investors hold the controlling interest.



“For us, we are advocating that because the company is about a three-in-one company, so let them buy up to 51 per cent. Let the government retain 49 per cent as it is in NLNG,” he said.



According to Osifo, private majority ownership would reduce government interference in operational and investment decisions.

He said decisions on maintenance and other business activities would no longer have to go through government processes, including federal executive council approvals.



“Because by the time Shell, ENI, Total Energy come together and make decisions, because they have 51 per cent, the project must move forward,” he said.



He added that private investors would be more likely to make decisions based on commercial considerations rather than political sentiments, while increased investment could create jobs and improve the value of the government’s remaining stake.



Osifo, who is concluding his tenure as PENGASSAN president, said one of the major objectives of his administration was to protect the jobs of members and improve their remuneration.



He said the union had achieved both objectives despite the extensive divestments that occurred in Nigeria’s oil and gas industry.



“How do we protect the job of our members and how do we enhance their pay?” he said, identifying the question as one of the fundamentals of his administration.



According to him, no PENGASSAN member lost his or her job as a direct consequence of the recent divestments involving major international oil companies.



He cited the divestments involving ExxonMobil, Shell, Eni and other international oil companies, saying the union ensured that its members’ employment and remuneration were protected throughout the transactions.



“We were able not just to protect the job of our members, but we ensured that the remuneration, we ensured that the pay of our members was not only transferred, but improved upon,” he said.



On PENGASSAN’s relationship with Dangote Refinery, Osifo said the disagreement between the union and the company had been resolved through sustained engagement.



He disclosed that about 600 workers who were disengaged by the Dangote Group during the dispute had subsequently been recalled and returned to work at the refinery.



Osifo said PENGASSAN was committed to supporting the refinery because of its importance to Nigeria’s energy security and employment generation.

“We do everything possible to protect every company that is in the space of the Nigerian oil and gas industry. Because Dangote Refinery will survive for us to have members there,” he said.



He welcomed the company’s plan to double the capacity of the refinery, saying the expansion would strengthen Nigeria’s energy security while creating additional employment opportunities.



Osifo said the relationship between PENGASSAN and the Dangote Group had now become “robust”, compared with the situation about a year earlier.

The TUC president also assessed the impact of the PIA, describing the legislation as a major reform that had delivered some important changes in the oil and gas sector.



He said PENGASSAN was initially excited when the PIA was passed in August 2021 because of its potential to transform the industry.



According to him, the creation of the upstream regulator and the midstream and downstream regulator, as well as the transformation of NNPC from a corporation into a commercially oriented company, were among the key achievements of the legislation.



He said the profitability recorded by NNPC after the PIA represented another significant development.



“20, 30, 40 years before PIA, they were always making losses. But after PIA, they started making profit. So, to that extent, you could say that there is some level of success,” he said.



He also cited the Host Community Development Trust (HCDT) and the Frontier Exploration Fund (FEF) as other areas where the PIA had made an impact.



However, Osifo said policy inconsistency remained a major challenge to the investment climate in the sector. He argued that the PIA should have been allowed to operate for at least five years before significant changes were introduced.



He expressed concern over the movement of fiscal provisions from the PIA to the Nigeria Revenue Service (NRS) legislation, saying such developments could create uncertainty for investors.



“For us, it was quite worrisome because that didn’t send the right signal to investors,” he said.



Osifo said investors needed certainty about taxes, royalties and other fiscal obligations before committing funds to long-term oil and gas projects.



“For an investor to know that I’m investing $10 million today, and this $10 million is the amount of money that I’m going to pay as taxes… investors need that certainty for them to invest,” he said.



He added that oil and gas investments often take several years before they begin to yield returns, making regulatory stability particularly important.

World.title: Geregu Defaults on N40 Billion Bond Payment 8 Months After Otedola’s Exit
World.content:
•NERC sacks Kaduna Disco board over N456.5bn debt

•Says Disco owes NBET N415.5bn, NISO N41bn

Emmanuel Addeh in Abuja





Geregu Power Plc has missed a scheduled payment on its N40.09 billion bond obligations, heightening investor concerns over the financial position of the power Generation Company (Genco), less than a year after the change of leadership at the organisation.

Specifically, the default, disclosed in an updated listing status by FMDQ Securities Exchange, comes about eight months after billionaire businessman, Femi Otedola, exited the company in a landmark $750 million transaction that transferred his controlling interest to MA’AM Energy Limited in December 2025.

Also, the Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission (NERC) yesterday announced the dissolution of the board of Kaduna Electricity Distribution Plc (KAEDC), citing prolonged financial and regulatory defaults, amounting to approximately N456.5 billion as of May 2026.

The Geregu transaction involved the sale of Otedola’s 95 per cent stake in Amperion Power Distribution Company Limited to MA’AM Energy Limited, effectively transferring the indirect controlling interest in the firm to the Abuja-based energy company. MA’AM Energy is involved in electricity generation and supply, energy trading and marketing.

Following the transaction, Senator Abdulaziz Yari emerged as chairman of the Geregu Power board, while a number of new directors were appointed, including Usman Gur Mohammed, Sani Jaafaru and Uzoamaka Adogu.

The acquisition was financed by a consortium of Nigerian banks led by Zenith Bank, with Blackbirch Capital acting as financial adviser.

Geregu Power was listed on the NGX four years ago amid strong investor expectations about the growth potential of Nigeria’s power market, where demand for electricity remains substantially higher than available generation.

But FMDQ classified the status of Geregu Power’s Series 1 bond as “credit default in the 8th coupon payment and 4th bullet principal repayment”, indicating that the company failed to meet two debt service obligations falling due under the bond structure.

The bond, valued at N40.09 billion, was issued on July 28, 2022, under Geregu Power’s N100 billion debt issuance programme at a fixed coupon rate of 14.50 per cent. It has a seven-year tenor and was structured to provide semi-annual coupon payments alongside scheduled principal repayments, with final maturity due on July 28, 2029.

The missed payments therefore represent a significant development occurring midway through the instrument’s life, rather than a maturity-related obligation, raising questions about the company’s immediate liquidity and debt-servicing capacity.

The development also coincides with a dramatic deterioration in Geregu Power’s financial performance, with the company reporting an 88 per cent decline in profit after tax and a 79 per cent fall in revenue in the first half of 2026.

Geregu Power’s profit after tax fell to N2.54 billion in the six months ended June 30, 2026, from N20.27 billion recorded in the corresponding period of 2025. Revenue also plunged to N18.65 billion from N87.63 billion a year earlier, representing a decline of 78.71 per cent.

The contraction became particularly severe in the second quarter, when the power generation company recorded turnover of only N419.1 million, compared with N55.87 billion in Q2 2025, representing a collapse of almost 99 per cent in quarterly turnover and underscoring the extent of the disruption to the company’s operations and cash generation during the period.

The latest figures are also a sharp reversal from Geregu Power’s expectations earlier in the year. The company had projected Q1 2026 revenue of N57.11 billion, compared with N31.75 billion in Q1 2025, while its projected profit after tax of N12.02 billion was also above the N10.43 billion recorded in the first quarter of 2025.

Instead, the company’s first-half performance came in substantially below both its previous-year results and its own earlier projections.

However, Geregu Power has attributed the operational disruption to a major turbine maintenance programme estimated at N61.47 billion.

The extensive overhaul, THISDAY learnt, is intended to preserve the long-term integrity of the generating assets and improve their availability. But the temporary loss of generating capacity has severely affected electricity output, revenue and, ultimately, cash flows available for debt servicing.

But despite the sharp deterioration in its operating performance, Geregu Power retained some balance-sheet support during the period, including financial asset impairment reversals amounting to N16.12 billion. Its total liabilities also declined to N239.33 billion during the period.

However, the bond default suggests that the company’s immediate cash-flow position remains under pressure, regardless of the longer-term value of its assets or its balance-sheet position.

The development is likely to draw particular attention from bondholders, who will be watching whether Geregu Power is able to cure the default within any applicable grace period and provide greater clarity on the timing for the restoration of its generating capacity.

GCR Ratings, however, has maintained a more positive long-term assessment of the company, affirming Geregu Power’s national scale long-term issuer rating at ‘A(NG)’ with a Stable Outlook.

The rating agency’s position reflects an expectation that the company’s operating performance will recover as the turbine overhauls are completed and its available generating capacity returns.

The rating outlook provides some counterweight to the immediate concerns generated by the missed debt payments, suggesting that the deterioration is viewed as potentially temporary and linked substantially to the maintenance-related reduction in generation.

For investors in the company’s equity, however, the market has begun to reflect some of the concerns surrounding Geregu Power’s deteriorating performance. Already, the company’s share price has fallen 27.67 per cent since the beginning of the year, declining from N1,141.50 to N825.70 as of Friday, August 7.

The decline indicated that investors have been reassessing the company’s earnings prospects at a time when its revenue has contracted sharply and its ability to meet debt obligations has come under pressure.

Meanwhile, the Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission (NERC) yesterday announced the dissolution of the board of Kaduna Electricity Distribution Plc (KAEDC) over prolonged financial and regulatory defaults, amounting to approximately N456.5 billion as of May 2026.

The commission, in Order No. NERC/2026/086, signed by its Chairman, Dr Musiliu Oseni and Commissioner in charge of Legal, Licensing and Compliance, Dafe Akpeneye, said KAEDC owed N415.5 billion to the Nigerian Bulk Electricity Trading Plc (NBET) and another N41 billion to the Nigerian Independent System Operator (NISO).

It further disclosed that the Disco had accumulated other non-market statutory and third-party obligations totalling N14.26 billion.

The latest intervention by NERC is not the first time the regulator has had to step in to address the ownership and management crisis at KAEDC, having intervened two years ago following concerns over the performance of its then core investor, Northwest Power Limited, amid the company’s deteriorating financial and operational position.

The intervention eventually paved the way for ASI Engineering Limited to assume operational control of the Disco in June 2024. The change was intended to provide a fresh start for KAEDC and address longstanding challenges around investment, electricity losses, market remittances and operational performance.

However, the latest regulatory order shows that the change in core investor and operational control has failed to deliver the expected turnaround.

But according to the regulator, KAEDC’s financial position even deteriorated further after ASI Engineering Limited took over operations in June 2024, with the company accruing additional market debt of more than N118.6 billion by May 2026.

NERC said its inquiry found KAEDC to be in a ‘grave situation’ characterised by prolonged regulatory and market default, inadequate investment, weak operational and commercial performance, insufficient assets relative to liabilities and an inability to present a credible pathway to sustainable recovery.

The commission said ASI and KAEDC had also persistently failed to furnish NBET and NISO with acceptable and credible payment bank guarantees required under the Vesting Contract and the Nigerian Electricity Supply Industry (NESI) market rules.

A THISDAY review of the document showed that the severity of the financial crisis was reflected in KAEDC’s 2025 remittance performance. The NERC document indicated that the Disco collected N51.39 billion during the year against adjusted market invoices of N80.44 billion but remitted only N33.73 billion.

This left a market shortfall of N46.71 billion, with KAEDC achieving only 41.93 per cent market remittance performance for the year.

The Disco’s operational performance was similarly poor. NERC said its Aggregate Technical, Commercial and Collection (ATC&C) losses stood at 71.88 per cent during the 2025 review period, meaning the company accounted for only about 28.2 per cent of the energy received and delivered to end-use customers.

The commission also faulted ASI’s investment performance, saying actual capital expenditure in 2025 was approximately N2.48 billion against a minimum requirement of N24.51 billion. This represented only about 10 per cent of the required capital expenditure, with NERC noting that the performance was achieved only through commission derogations and forbearances.

“The commission, following its inquiry and consultation undertaken with key industry stakeholders including the Bureau of Public Enterprises (BPE), finds that Kaduna Electricity Distribution Plc (KAEDC or the Licensee) is in a grave situation characterised by prolonged regulatory and market default, inadequate investment, weak operational and commercial performance, insufficient assets relative to liabilities, and inability to present a credible pathway to sustainable recovery,” the order stated.

According to NERC, meter coverage also remained low, ranging between 33.26 per cent and 35.54 per cent since ASI’s takeover. The annual metering rate for 2025 stood at 34.42 per cent. NERC said the poor performance persisted despite significant regulatory and government interventions.

It disclosed that approximately N6.58 billion in regulatory derogations had been granted to KAEDC between January 2024 and May 2026, while aggregate federal government intervention disbursements to the Disco since July 2018 totalled approximately N53.79 billion.

The commission said it had also notified KAEDC’s major shareholders and Afrexim of imminent regulatory intervention after the company failed to provide a credible sustainability plan.

At a June 11, 2026 meeting involving key stakeholders, the core investor, it said, requested a 24-month extension to stabilise cash flow, prioritise critical investments and achieve measurable performance improvements, including a pathway to full market remittance.

But NERC, BPE and Afrexim, however, determined that another extension of comparable duration was not justifiable because of the continuing risks to end-use customers and the electricity market.

The commission also said ASI failed to provide a credible plan to support its request for the 24-month extension. Consequently, NERC said it invoked its powers under sections 75 to 79 of the Electricity Act 2023 to intervene in KAEDC.

“KAEDC’s board of directors is hereby dissolved. All directors of KAEDC are removed from office, and the existing board stands dissolved pursuant to section 75 of the EA. The Commission has notified the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC) and other relevant stakeholders of the dissolution of the board,” it stated.

The commission subsequently appointed a seven-member interim board of special directors to oversee the utility during the transition.

The interim board is chaired by Dr Abdullahi Garba, while Mr Francis Agoha, Mr Aliyu Aliyu, Maj. Gen. Henry Ayamasaowei (rtd) and Dr Haliru Dikko were appointed as special directors.

Also, Dr Ayodeji Gbeleyi was appointed as special director representing the BPE, while Dr Abubakar Hashidu was appointed special director for an initial six-month term and simultaneously designated administrator subject to NERC’s review.

NERC stated that the objective was to preserve KAEDC as a going concern and achieve a transparent transition to a credible core investor within 12 months through a sale process based on the highest and best price offered.

As part of the transition, Afrexim, in coordination with NERC, is to lead an open, competitive and transparent process to secure a replacement core investor and present the preferred investor to the Commission for approval.

NERC further directed the Administrator, BPE, NBET, NISO and other material creditors to reconcile KAEDC’s liabilities and file a liability management plan within 90 days of the commencement of the order.

World.title: Bamaiyi, Turaki, Bala Lead PDP Faction to Back Governor Idris in Kebbi State Election
World.content:
Onuminya Innocent in Sokoto





The re-election bid of Kebbi State Governor, Comrade Nasir Idris, received a major boost recently following the declaration of support by a strong faction of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) in the state.

Hundreds of PDP stakeholders converged at the Birnin Kebbi residence of former Chief of Army Staff, Lt. Gen. Ishaya Bamaiyi (rtd), weekend, to announce their alignment with the governor ahead of the 2027 general election.

Among those present were loyalists of the PDP 2015 governorship candidate, General Bello Sarkin Yaki; former Minister of Special Duties, Kabiru Tanimu Turaki, SAN, and former Minister of Foreign Affairs, Alhaji Buhari Bala.

Bamaiyi said despite the current crisis rocking the PDP at the national level, progressive politicians in the state could not afford to remain passive.

He noted that the visible transformation witnessed in Birnin Kebbi and Idris’s commitment to critical infrastructure projects informed their decision to support his continuity in office.

“For the 2027 elections, we are now fully committed to the victory of Governor Nasir Idris, Kauran Gwandu,” Bamaiyi declared.

He, however, added that the group would remain within the PDP, citing the dynamic nature of democracy.

Also speaking, Alhaji Buhari Bala, said with their pedigree in Nigeria’s political evolution, they could not afford to “sidon-look” in the face of what he described as patriotic and selfless leadership being exhibited by the governor.

Bala stressed that the group’s decision was based on performance, unity, and the need to ensure sustained development in Kebbi rather than partisan considerations.

Governor Idris, however, thanked the PDP stakeholders and their teeming followers for the confidence reposed in his administration and leadership style.

World.title: NARD to FCTA: Withdraw Queries or Face Nationwide Industrial Action
World.content:
Ayodeji Ake





The Nigerian Association of Resident Doctors (NARD) has threatened to embark on nationwide industrial action if the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) Administration fails to withdraw queries issued to members of the Executive Council of the Association of Resident Doctors (ARD), FCT chapter.

NARD, in a statement signed by its President, Dr. Mohammad Usman Suleiman; Secretary-General, Dr. Shuaibu Ibrahim, and Publicity and Social Secretary, Dr. Abdulmajid Yahya Ibrahim, accused the FCT authorities of victimising the affected doctors for communicating the position of the national body on its planned industrial action.

The statement followed the issuance of queries to members of the ARD FCT Executive Council after the association notified the authorities of its planned nationwide industrial action scheduled to commence on August 10.

NARD described the queries as “unwarranted and unacceptable victimisation,” insisting that the affected doctors were only carrying out their responsibilities as elected representatives of their colleagues.

The association called on the FCT Minister, Nyesom Wike, to urgently intervene and direct the Chairman of the FCT Civil Service Commission, Engr. Emeka Ezeh, to withdraw the queries.

NARD also urged the minister to reprimand officials of the FCT Hospitals Management Board whom it accused of involvement in the issuance of the queries.

According to the doctors’ body, the affected resident doctors should not be subjected to intimidation, harassment or punitive administrative measures for communicating decisions of their national union through appropriate channels.

“NARD considers the issuance of queries to union representatives over the communication of a planned national action deeply troubling and capable of unnecessarily escalating tension and undermining industrial harmony within the FCT health sector,” the association said.

The association warned that it would not fold its arms while its members or elected representatives were allegedly victimised over legitimate union activities.

It said any action against members of the ARD FCT Executive Council in the course of discharging their responsibilities would be regarded as an issue concerning the entire NARD family.

NARD therefore demanded the immediate withdrawal of the queries, warning that failure to do so would lead to further lawful collective action.

It said the first step would be a national protest in Abuja, with resident doctors mobilised to publicly express their opposition to what it described as the victimisation of their representatives.

“Should the queries remain in force thereafter, a national industrial action will immediately follow,” NARD warned.

The association stressed that its position was not intended as a threat but as a declaration of its resolve to protect the rights, dignity and legitimate interests of its members through lawful and constitutionally recognised means.

NARD maintained that it remained committed to constructive engagement, meaningful dialogue and peaceful resolution of disputes with government at all levels.

It, however, argued that meaningful dialogue would not thrive in an atmosphere where duly elected union representatives were subjected to victimisation or intimidation for carrying out legitimate responsibilities.

The association expressed optimism that an intervention by the FCT Minister would help prevent unnecessary escalation, preserve industrial harmony and demonstrate the administration’s commitment to a fair and respectful relationship with healthcare professionals.

NARD reiterated its demand for the immediate withdrawal of the queries and an end to any further victimisation arising from the matter.

The association also reaffirmed its commitment to dialogue and peaceful engagement, but warned that it would not compromise the dignity, welfare and legitimate rights of resident doctors.

World.title: Sheikh Yahaya Jingir’s Comments Will Hurt Tinubu in 2027, Fani-Kayode Warns
World.content:
Chuks Okocha in Abuja





Nigeria’s Ambassador-designate to South Africa, Femi Fani-Kayode, has warned that recent comments by Islamic cleric, Sheikh Yahaya Jingir, in favour of retaining a Muslim-Muslim presidential ticket could undermine President Bola Tinubu’s re-election bid in 2027.

Fani-Kayode said Jingir’s position risked alienating Christian voters, deepening religious divisions and providing opposition parties with a campaign issue they could deploy against the All Progressives Congress ahead of the presidential election.

The former minister made the remarks in a Facebook post yesterday, reacting to comments attributed to Jingir at an event in Kano, where the cleric reportedly advocated the continued adoption of Muslim-Muslim presidential tickets and identified himself as a strong supporter of the arrangement.

Fani-Kayode said the remarks had generated concern among Nigerians across religious lines, claiming that he received more than 100 calls and messages from Christians and Muslims after the comments were published.

He said he was particularly disturbed by the reaction of the Kano State governor, whom he accused of openly cheering and celebrating Jingir’s position.

“There is only one thing worse and that saddened me more than what he said and that is to have seen my friend and brother, the Governor of Kano State, cheering him on and celebrating it,” Fani-Kayode said.

He warned political actors against turning religious identity into an instrument of political mobilisation, arguing that doing so could aggravate existing tensions and have consequences beyond the 2027 election.

“We will not keep quiet and watch our faith being dragged all over the floor because of politics. Matters of faith and salvation are far more important than anything we see or get in this world.

“Politics and earthly power come and go but faith and the afterlife is eternal. This divisive rhetoric has to stop and we should stop playing with fire,” he said.

According to Fani-Kayode, Jingir’s comments were particularly ill-advised given Nigeria’s sizeable Christian population and the international controversy surrounding allegations of religious persecution in the country.

“You do not talk like that in a country with over 120 million Christians. This is especially so when we are already being falsely accused of Christian genocide and of harbouring an agenda to Islamise the country and do away with all Christians by some of our American friends,” he said.

He argued that the cleric’s comments could inadvertently lend credibility to narratives that the government and its supporters have consistently rejected, while also weakening the ruling party’s electoral prospects.

“Jingir is not only feeding into that false narrative with his reckless words, but he is also endangering the chances of our candidates in the 2027 presidential election because in order for us to win, we need BOTH Muslim AND Christian votes.

“What he has done is given the opposition something to hold on to and use against us and this is unfortunate,” he said.

World.title: Ezekwesili Decries Failure of Governance, Says Nigeria Needs Rebirth
World.content:
Funmi Ogundare





Former Minister of Education and Chairperson, School of Politics, Policy and Governance, Dr. Oby Ezekwesili, yesterday cautioned Nigerians against making the 2027 presidential election the sole focus of national discourse, arguing that the country’s more fundamental challenge is the failure of political and governance system.

Ezekwesili, who spoke during an interview on AriseTV PrimeTime, explained that Nigeria urgently needs a fundamental conversation about its future, including the establishment of shared national values, a common vision and a political system capable of delivering meaningful development to citizens.

She argued that the country’s recurring focus on elections had failed to address the structural problems responsible for its deteriorating political, economic and social conditions.

According to her, Nigerians must challenge the belief that the current state of the country represents their destiny, insisting that the situation was the product of deliberate political choices and systems that could be changed.

“The greatest tragedy of the country is this resignation that this is our destiny. I say no. This is by design. It is not our destiny,” she stated.

Ezekwesili said the country needed a national conversation that would lead to an agreement on shared values and a national vision, noting that such an understanding should ultimately form the basis for a new constitutional arrangement.

She lamented the absence of a strong social contract, social cohesion and social capital in Nigeria, saying these deficiencies had continued to deepen ethnic, religious and other divisions.

According to her, Nigerians needs a compelling national vision that would give citizens a reason to identify with the Nigerian project beyond their ethnic or religious identities.

She said patriotism should not be interpreted as blind support for the existing political arrangement, stressing that criticism of poor governance was not equivalent to opposition to Nigeria.

The former minister also criticised the political class for failing to facilitate the fundamental conversation required to move Nigeria from being merely a geographical entity to a cohesive nation.

She argued that since independence, Nigeria had not adequately undertaken the kind of national dialogue required to establish shared values, agree on a national vision and develop a constitution based on that consensus.

“We should have really had a conversation that would get us to the place where we would agree that these are shared values; this is our national vision, and then come up with a constitution based on that,” she said.

On the 2027 presidential election, Ezekwesili reaffirmed her support for the Nigeria Democratic Congress ( NDC) presidential candidate, Peter Obi, saying her position was based on her assessment of leadership qualities rather than political affiliation.

She explained that in 2023 she assessed the major presidential candidates using the criteria of character, competence and capacity, and concluded that Obi scored considerably higher than the other leading contenders.

“I was going to stand with Governor Obi. I haven’t seen that anything has really significantly changed,” she said.

However, she maintained that Nigerians should not lose sight of the larger national questions simply because of the approaching election.

On the possibility of Obi overcoming the advantages of the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC), including incumbency, political structures and financial resources, Ezekwesili acknowledged the challenges but said the electorate could still create a political turning point.

She noted that while incumbents traditionally deployed their advantages to influence electoral outcomes, there were moments when citizens reached a point where they rejected the prevailing political trajectory.

“There are situations where the people vote for themselves. They come to that point where they say, ‘Okay, you’ve had it. You’ve really had it. We can’t continue on this trajectory because it actually is too injurious,’” she said.

She also acknowledged the severe economic pressure facing millions of Nigerians, particularly those living on low household incomes, saying such circumstances could influence voters’ choices during elections.

She, however, warned that the immediate economic incentives available to citizens should not permanently determine the future of the country, arguing that many Nigerians were compelled by economic hardship to prioritise short-term survival over long-term national interests.

The chairperson further criticised sections of the middle class for failing to invest sufficiently in building a sustainable Nigeria, noting that increasing numbers of families were looking abroad for better opportunities for their children.

According to her, Nigeria needed a constituency of citizens willing to make sacrifices and demand fundamental reforms rather than merely adapting to a dysfunctional system.

She cited Kenya as an example of a country that had confronted fundamental questions about its political and constitutional arrangements, arguing that Nigeria could also move beyond its existential nation-building challenges if it was willing to engage in a genuine national conversation.

She stated: “the Nigerian political class had resisted conversations around restructuring, constitutional reform and competitiveness because the existing arrangement continued to serve the interests of political elites.”

On what Obi would need to do differently in 2027 to transform his significant following into a nationwide electoral coalition, Ezekwesili said the task would require more than inspirational speeches.

“It is not merely providing inspiration of speeches. It is really very technical because it is granular, and it is really about being strategic,” she said.

She stressed that any attempt to transform Nigeria’s political system must be anchored on a broader national project capable of addressing the country’s governance failures and restoring citizens’ confidence in the Nigerian state.

World.title: Umahi: FG to Deploy Guards to Protect Abuja-Kaduna Highway
World.content:
•Lagos-Calabar coastal highway will be completed, says minister

Emmanuel Addeh in Abuja





The federal government will deploy security guards to protect infrastructure along the Abuja-Kaduna-Zaria-Kano superhighway from vandalism, Minister of Works, David Umahi, said yesterday.

Umahi disclosed this when he received the leadership of the National Association of Nigerian Students (NANS) on a courtesy visit to the ministry.

He said the measure became necessary following attempts by vandals to damage newly constructed sections of major federal highways.

“I just came back from Lagos when we inaugurated the coastal highway guard. We are going to inaugurate this Abuja, Kaduna, Zaria, Kano Superhighway. I saw people digging the concrete to remove rods. But I’ve said that if they can commit to that level, just out of it, a meaningful job,” Umahi said.

The minister said the Abuja-Kaduna-Zaria-Kano corridor, covering about 750 kilometres of carriageway, had received more than N200 billion in government funding, while the current projects on the corridor were valued at N752 billion, with over 80 per cent paid.

“We are believing that by November, the entire stretch will have been completed,” he said, adding that solar lights would also be installed along the highway.

Umahi said the government’s road projects had created employment opportunities across the country, noting that “there is no site in all these projects here that has less than 1,000 normal people.”

He also highlighted other ongoing projects, including the Sokoto-Zamfara-Zaria corridor, the Benue-9th Mile road and the Port Harcourt-Bonny road, which he said had been completed.

On the Port Harcourt-Bonny project, he said: “That project is completed. 39.7 kilometres. Fully done.” He added: “The people of Bonny are very happy. They are no longer dying in the sea. They are now driving through the land,” he added.

The minister also defended the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway against criticism, insisting that the project would be completed. “That is being unfair. That is being unrealistic. That project will be done,” he said.

Umahi urged NANS to participate actively in monitoring federal projects and approved support for the association to undertake project monitoring nationwide.

“If you help us to monitor these projects, please no blackmail, no intimidation, no altercation with contractors. Every responsibility, I take responsibility. And if you do this intelligently and honestly, we are partners,” he said.

He also urged young Nigerians to focus on productivity and skills acquisition, saying, “We need to do things with our hands.”

The minister further urged students to engage the government on national issues based on evidence rather than social media narratives. “If you say that the President is not doing well, what is your own alternative?” he asked.

On his part, NANS President, Akinteye Babatunde, commended Umahi for the ministry’s infrastructure projects, saying good roads were essential to students’ academic activities and mobility.

“For students, infrastructure is not an abstract concept. A bad road can mean arriving late for an examination. A bad road can increase the cost of transportation to school. An inaccessible community can limit educational opportunities,” Babatunde said.

He added that roads being constructed across the country would connect students, communities and businesses to wider opportunities.

“The roads we are building today will help lead this administration. They will carry students to schools, farmers to markets, workers to their places of employment, businesses to their customers and families to their destinations. That is the significance of infrastructure,” he said.

World.title: 2027 Polls: Kano Emirate, Islamic Scholars Call for National Prayers, Peaceful Election
World.content:
Michael Olugbode in Abuja





The Kano Emirate and Islamic scholars have called on Nigerians to intensify prayers for a peaceful, credible and successful 2027 general election.

They also warned that the country’s stability would depend largely on the ability of citizens and leaders to embrace tolerance, discipline and responsible conduct.

They, therefore, urge Nigerians to reject intolerance, violence, while telling Qur’anic graduates to become ambassadors of peace

The appeal was made at a Qur’anic graduation ceremony marking the completion of the recitation and memorisation of the Holy Qur’an, where traditional and religious leaders used the occasion to call for stronger moral upbringing of Nigerian children ahead of another politically sensitive electoral cycle.

Representing the Emir of Kano at the ceremony, the Sadauki of Kano, Awal Ado Bayero, congratulated the graduates and their parents, but charged the students to see the completion of their Qur’anic studies as the beginning of a lifelong responsibility to live by the values they had learnt.

Bayero said the teachings of the Qur’an could play an important role in promoting peaceful coexistence, good character and responsible citizenship, particularly at a time when the country was preparing for the 2027 elections.

“As we approach the 2027 general elections, we pray that the children will continue to pray for the country and that Nigeria will have a successful, peaceful and credible election,” he said.

He urged the graduates to remain committed to Qur’anic recitation and memorisation, while calling on parents and older generations to ensure that the values contained in the Holy Book were transmitted to their children and grandchildren.

The call soon assumed wider significance as other speakers at the ceremony linked the moral upbringing of children to the broader challenge of building a peaceful and secure Nigeria.

Katsina State First Lady, Dr. Aisha Bala Muhammed, who was represented at the event, described the completion of the Qur’an as a major achievement and urged the graduates to make its teachings the foundation of their lives.

“May He make the Quran a light in your heart, a guide throughout your life, and a source of peace and blessings for you and your family,” she said.

Similarly, the wife of the Speaker of the Bauchi State House of Assembly, Hajia Abi Hafsat Abubakar Y. Suleiman, said the programme was designed to strengthen the religious and moral upbringing of children and prepare them to become responsible members of society.

The Principal of the Abuja National Mosque Academy, Dr Shehu Usman Mohamad, said the essence of Qur’anic education was not simply to produce children who could recite and memorise the Holy Book, but to raise Muslims capable of applying its teachings to everyday life.

World.title: How much it costs to: Take the family to watch Springboks play the All Blacks
World.content:
Take a look at the estimated cost of taking a family of four to watch the Springboks play the All Blacks in South Africa. Image: ChatGPT

Taking a family of four to watch the Springboks play the All Blacks will cost anything between R3 400 to over R11 000 – for tickets alone.

This is of course dependent on the match, seating choice and other costs.

Factoring in transport, food, drinks etc and the total outing skyrockets even higher.



SPRINGBOKS TICKET PRICES

The Springboks will host the All Blacks in three blockbuster Tests in the coming weeks.

Take a look at the matches, cost of tickets and a breakdown of what this would cost a family of four:

Venue City Tickets (per person) Family of 4 Ellis Park Johannesburg R1 650 – R2 850 R6,600 – R11 400 Cape Town Stadium Cape Town R1 650 – R4 000 R6 600 – R16 000 FNB Stadium Johannesburg R850 – R4 000 R3 400 – R16 000

The most economical tickets priced between R850 to R1 650 typically sell out quickly, leaving mid- and premium categories as the only options.

OTHER COSTS TO FACTOR IN

TRANSPORT

Durban to Johannesburg (Ellis Park/FNB Stadium): ± R2 000 petrol return or ± R6 000 flights for four.

Durban to Cape Town (Cape Town Stadium): ± R3 000 petrol return or ± R8 000 flights for four.

Local travel (Durban to Kings Park for franchise matches): ± R200 petrol/parking.



FOOD AND DRINKS

Stadium snacks and drinks average R150 per person.

Family of four: ± R600 to R1 000 depending on choices.

MERCHANDISE

Official Springbok jerseys cost around R2 500 each.

Full family set: ±R10 000

Therefore, the cost of tickets to take your family to watch a Springboks vs All Blacks match ranges between R3 400 to over R11 000 with variable costs amounting to R800 to ‘as much as you can afford to spend’ depending on the transport, merchandise and personal preferences.

World.title: WHY you weren’t paid: SASSA fourth payment date explained
World.content:
The South African is inundated with messages regarding the SASSA fourth payment date. Every month, like clockwork, the same panic and anger spreads through beneficiaries. Grant day comes and goes, but the money isn’t there.

So, let’s get to the bottom of the question: Why hasn’t your SASSA grant been paid? And what can you do about it …

As we all know, the South African Social Security Agency follows a fixed payment order each month. Older Persons Grants go out first. Disability & War Veterans follow a day later. Children’s Grants – including the Child Support Grant and Foster Child Grant – come after that. That’s the cycle most people know. Three days, three categories, done …



Then there’s day four. Next month it falls on Monday 7 September 2026. This date isn’t for everyone. It’s reserved for beneficiaries SASSA flagged for grant review or eLife Certification. If your name lands on this list, you will not get paid with everyone else in your category. You get paid on the fourth day instead, once all is rectified.

SAME PROBLEM EACH MONTH

It’s nothing personal if you’re called in for review. But not resolving it in time could cost you … Image: File

However, SASSA National Spokesperson Paseka Letsatsi says the agency keeps running into the same problem each month. Beneficiaries under review don’t realise what the SASSA fourth payment date is for, or when it is. So, they see no payment on the normal date, assume the worst, and call or flood SASSA offices in-person in a panic. Moreover, they don’t realise these grant reviews aren’t random or malicious.

SASSA runs continuous checks on beneficiary eligibility, verifying income, life status and other qualifying details for everyone. eLife Certification is part of that, too, confirming a beneficiary is still alive and still meets the criteria for their grant. The agency leaned hard into the practice in 2025. More than 291 000 beneficiaries were identified for review and as many as 34 600 grants were summarily cancelled, according to figures from the Finance Minister’s 2026 Budget.



YOU’VE DONE NOTHING WRONG

Critically, none of that means a flagged beneficiary has done anything wrong (until proven otherwise). It means SASSA wants/needs updated documentation before the SASSA fourth payment dates rolls around. You must visit your nearest SASSA office during the month to complete the review. Skip this and SASSA can suspend your grant in the following payment cycle.

Leave it unresolved for any longer, and the grant can be cancelled outright. Beneficiaries who are bedridden or otherwise unable to get to an office in person can have alternative arrangements made with a doctor’s note and documents verified by a commissioner of oaths (SAPS police station).

The agency is mandated by the National Treasury to try and save every rand and cent it can in the fight against fraudulent grants. Image: File

So, if payment hasn’t landed for your , don’t panic on day one. Check whether you’ve been contacted about a review or eLife Certification first. Make sure your cellphone number on file with SASSA is current. The bulk SMS notifications that explain all of this are useless if they’re going to a number you haven’t used in years.



Get to your nearest office before month-end and complete the review. You will need to produce all the same documents – and copies – just like you did when you first applied to prove your identity, assets and means (if applicable). The alternative, ignoring it, means payment may not come at all next month.

But what do you think? Have you successfully resolved a SASSA fourth payment date dispute? Please share your thoughts and experiences for other beneficiaries in the comments section below …

World.title: Tuesday and Wednesday night: 8 Betway Premiership fixtures
World.content:
Lebohang Maboe plays for Kaizer Chiefs in the Betway Premiership against Kruger United. Image: Kaizer Chiefs media

All eight Betway Premiership fixtures are scheduled for 19:30. Mamelodi Sundowns, Orlando Pirates and Kaizer Chiefs headline the two-day programme.

MAMELODI SUNDOWNS VISIT TS GALAXY

Kabo Yellowfinally begin their Betway Premiership campaign on Tuesday night. The reigning African champions travel to face TS Galaxy at Mbombela Stadium.

The fixture was originally the subject of a venue request from TS Galaxy. The club wanted to move the match to Solomon Mahlangu Stadium, but the Premier Soccer League rejected the request. The game will therefore go ahead in Nelspruit.



Also read: Bafana Bafana news: Mosimane rejects R5 million-a-year salary

Polokwane City will host Stellenbosch FC at Seshego Stadium, while Chippa United welcome Richards Bay to Dobsonville Stadium. At Royal Bafokeng Stadium, Marumo Gallants face newly promoted Kruger United.

Wednesday brings another set of heavyweight fixtures. Orlando Pirates travel to Durban to face AmaZulu at Hollywoodbets Kings Park Stadium after opening their title defence with a 2-0 win over Milford.

The Buccaneers will want another positive result, but AmaZulu will provide a much tougher test on home soil. The Durban side will be determined to make their home advantage count against the defending champions.

KAIZER CHIEFS HOST SEKHUHUNE UNITED IN THE BETWAY PREMIERSHIP

Kaizer Chiefs return to FNB Stadium on Wednesday when they face Sekhukhune United. The Amakhosi will be looking to continue their strong start after beating Kruger United 3-1 in their opening league fixture.

The match comes just days after Kaizer Chiefs suffered a 1-0 defeat to Lamontville Golden Arrows in the MTN8 quarter-final. Sekhukhune United will therefore provide another test as Chiefs look to quickly recover from that disappointment.



There is also a KwaZulu-Natal derby at Chatsworth Stadium, where Durban City take on Lamontville Golden Arrows. Golden Arrows enter the match with confidence after eliminating Chiefs from the MTN8.
