The price of homes fell in six Dutch councils in the second quarter of 2026, up from just one three months earlier, a sign that the housing market is levelling off.

Figures from national statistics agency CBS and the Land Registry showed the biggest drop was in Noord-Beveland, in Zeeland, where prices were 5.1% lower than a year earlier.

Prices also fell in Ouder-Amstel (-2.8%), Hillegom (-2.5%), Valkenswaard, Veldhoven and IJsselstein. In the first quarter, only Gulpen-Wittem in Limburg had seen a fall.

Nationally, prices were still 4.2% higher than a year earlier – the tenth quarter in a row of increases, though the pace has slowed.

The sharpest rises were in the rural east and north. Prices in Oost Gelre, in Gelderland, jumped 20.9%, followed by Voorst (19.4%) and Pekela (16.2%).

Among the four biggest cities, prices in Amsterdam rose 0.1%.

World.title: Police investigating three explosive attacks on pilates studio
World.content:
A pilates studio in Gelderland has been hit by three explosive attacks in six weeks, the most recent in the early hours of Monday, police have said.

The studio in Zevenaar, which opened a year ago, was first targeted on June 24, when a blast blew a window pane out of the front door and caused a fire to break out.

A witness saw a man in black clothing and a cap running from the scene immediately after the explosion, but police have not managed to trace him.

Five days later a second explosion blew a hole in the entrance. The word betalen (“pay”) was written three times on a window.

The most recent attack was at around 2.45am on Monday, when another explosion went off and a brick was hurled through a window, Omroep Gelderland reported. The explosion was heard throughout the neighbourhood.

The door and several windows of the building have been boarded up following the attacks. Police would not say if they were linked or if any arrests have been made.

World.title: Two men suspected of helping grave robber sell stolen valuables
World.content:
Two men have been questioned on suspicion of acting as accomplices for a man accused of stealing valuables from a cemetery in The Hague by selling the items to a gold dealer.

The 60-year-old man, who works as a shift manager at the city’s main cemetery on Kerkhoflaan, was arrested in June after police received a tip-off that items such as jewellery and gold fillings had been stolen during working hours.

The prosecution service confirmed on Monday that two other people who worked at the cemetery were suspected of money laundering “by selling valuable objects originating from the cemetery”.

The man was arrested after an inspection of the official register where second-hand and antique traders are required to log their purchases revealed that he had sold several items to a gold exchange bureau.

Prosecutors said there were no indications from the investigation so far that items had been stolen from other cemeteries in the city. The inquiry covers the period from 2023 until the man’s arrest.

The city council has launched its own internal inquiry and set up a hotline for families who were concerned that their relatives’ valuables may have been stolen. So far the hotline has received around 60 calls.

World.title: Scammers flood TikTok with fake student rental ads
World.content:
Hundreds of fake s for student rooms and rental homes are circulating on TikTok in an effort to defraud people looking for housing, according to an investigation by broadcaster NOS.

The scammers are also lifting listings from Pararius, one of the largest rental platforms in the Netherlands, and the company says it now wants TikTok to act. “We are completely fed up and want action from TikTok now,” Jasper de Groot, a Pararius spokesperson, told the broadcaster.

Some of the people who lose money come to Pararius believing they have rented through the site, De Groot said, because they have transferred a payment – only for it to reach a scammer instead.

Scams and complaints

The fraudsters copy photographs of real rooms from Pararius and reuse them in fake posts. Victims are typically asked to pay before they can view a property – a deposit, a viewing fee or a “reservation guarantee” – after which the money disappears.

The national student union, the LSVb, said it regularly hears from young people who get conned out of their money. “Sometimes a deposit is also demanded in advance and the room turns out not to exist at all,” said vice-chair Juliana Könning. “Students then lose their deposit of, say, three months’ rent.”

The Fraudehelpdesk, the national fraud reporting centre, received 175 reports in the first half of 2026 from people scammed through an , NOS Stories said, up from 21 in the previous six months.

International students are among those most exposed, unable to fall back on a parental home and often unfamiliar with their rights, the LSVb has warned in the past.

Platforms under pressure

TikTok said content used to defraud people is not allowed and that it removes such posts. The platform did not explain why it had not acted on the reports filed by Pararius.

After NOS Stories shared a number of fake s, the accounts behind them were taken down, but dozens of other scam accounts remained online.

Pararius said it had sent TikTok dossiers containing victims’ police reports and a registered letter, without success, and would take legal action against the platform. “It has to stop,” De Groot said.

Funda said it warns consumers but can do little because the fraud takes place elsewhere, while room-rental site Kamernet said it advises users to report suspicious posts and may pursue legal steps if they are not removed.

World.title: Perks of the job: making the most of your Dutch salary
World.content:
So you’ve got the job, you are moving to the Netherlands and you are ready to jump into your new life. Here is a guide from ABN Amro on some practical and financial matters you need to arrange, as well as some Dutch workplace benefits worth knowing about.

Get your finances set up

First things first – you need a current account so your employer can deposit your salary, and having a local account will make it easier to manage your day-to-day finances. Note, you must have a Dutch bank account to get paid by a Dutch employer.

ABN Amro, which has 25 years’ experience in helping expat clients, is currently offering up to €175 cashback to new account holders – a handy financial bonus, especially at the start of a new life in the Netherlands.

But what other financial things do you need to get sorted out? Apart from a current account, you might like to start saving, so opening a savings account at the same bank would be a sensible move.

You’ll also need insurance – you’ll find out very soon that the Dutch love insurance – and, of course, some insurance, such as health cover, is compulsory too. ABN Amro offers several insurance products that you should consider – from personal liability to contents and legal aid. If you take out three or more insurance policies with them, you will receive a 3% to 5% package discount. That’s another nice financial bonus.

Then there are work-related financial benefits.

Exploring Dutch employee benefits

One perk of a Dutch job that many people are not aware of to begin with is holiday pay, or vakantiegeld. All workers and benefit claimants in the Netherlands have the right to holiday pay, which is equivalent to 8% of their annual income.

The concept of holiday pay dates back to 1910 and the money was traditionally paid out at the end of May to make sure people actually used it to pay for a break.

By the way, by law you are entitled to at least 20 paid holiday days if you work a five-day week, but in most pay deals (CAOs), 25 paid days off or even more are the norm.

In some sectors you may also be entitled to a 13th month paid out in December. Some companies also have different ways of giving their staff a bonus, such as a fixed amount for reaching a performance target.

Travel allowances and company bikes

Your job may entitle you to help with the cost of getting to and from work. Employers are allowed to give staff a tax-free allowance of 23 cents per kilometre for using public transport or a car or bike to commute, or you may be entitled to a public transport card that offers discounted travel. You may even be able to get a company bike.

Every employer is different, so make sure you ask HR about the travel perks at your company.

Other job-related perks

You may find your company canteen is subsidised or even free. You may also be entitled to gym membership or other club activities, and by law, if you work remotely, you are entitled to €2.45 a day as a working-from-home allowance. Some companies also offer a training budget to keep your skills up to date or provide Dutch lessons for their international staff.

Many internationals are surprised by the extra payments and perks they are entitled to when working for a Dutch company, just as they are surprised by the strict Dutch work-life balance and the way most people head off home at 5pm and don’t answer their work phone at the weekend.

Make sure you don’t get any unwanted financial surprises by getting your money matters sorted out, and do feel free to put your questions to ABN Amro’s specialist support staff for internationals. Find out more about opening an ABN Amro bank account and how you can benefit from a €175 cashback offer. That’s a lot of takeaway lattes – also an essential part of Dutch working life!

World.title: Rotterdam night entry ban brings quiet, residents want it kept
World.content:
Residents of the Rotterdam neighbourhood De Esch say the nights have been quiet since a ban on entering the area took effect two weeks ago, but fear the disruption will return when it runs out in October.

A curfew for anyone without a good reason for being in the area was imposed on July 23, making it an offence to be on the streets from 11pm till 5am. The unprecedented move follows years of persistent anti-social behaviour in the area, usually by people who don’t live there.

Police stopped about 100 people during the first fortnight, though no fines have been issued yet – the penalty is expected to be more than €100.

Quiet nights

“The windows can just stay open all the time,” one resident told broadcaster NOS. “It was very quiet from night one.”

Another resident told regional broadcaster Rijnmond that before the ban she had been kept awake almost every night by shouting and car horns, even with earplugs, and had slept well for the first time in a long while.

The neighbourhood, home to more than 4,000 people, had put up with street races, drug use and prostitution at night for years. Police research found that most of those responsible came from outside De Esch.

Police and the council say the disruption has not moved to other areas, but both note that it is the holiday season and the picture may change.

After October

The ban runs for three months and can be extended by another three after consultation.

The residents’ committee wants the neighbourhood closed at night once it ends, with marshals at the entrances at weekends letting in only people with a reason to be there.

The neighbourhood council, which advises the city, is against that. “It restricts the movement of other Rotterdammers too much,” its chairman Christiaan de Jong told NOS.

He said he hoped instead that behaviour would change and the disruption would be less than before. The council says it is too early to discuss a permanent solution, and that no other part of Rotterdam needs the same measure.

World.title: German zeppelin takes to Dutch skies to measure air pollution
World.content:
People living in the Veluwe region near the German border have been surprised by the sight of a zeppelin hovering in the skies above their heads.

The airship took off from Essen, in the Ruhr area of North Rhine-Westphalia, and is being used to measure air pollution in an area on both sides of the border that covers Arnhem and Utrecht.

Scientists from Wageningen University & Research have equipped the balloon with instruments to measure levels of CO2 pollution, emissions and fine particles in the air, in a joint operation with German colleagues.

“The substances are partly produced by the forest and partly by traffic and industry,” researcher Michiel van der Molen told NOS. “Exactly how that works and how quickly it spreads is interesting, but mostly unknown.”

The zeppelin is due to pass over the area several times during the next week at a height of around 300 metres above ground level. Its path can be followed on Flightradar24 under the code DLZFN.

World.title: Thieves caught trying to retrieve cigarettes from police station
World.content:

Thieves broke into a police station in The Hague to try to retrieve a batch of illegal cigarettes that were seized in a raid on Friday.

Four suspects were arrested when they were caught while trying to throw boxes of cigarettes over the fence of the police compound on Zichtenburglaan at 4.45am on Saturday.

One of the boxes caught on the fence and burst open, scattering cigarettes over the ground just as officers arrived on the scene.

The suspects tried to escape by car, but were forced off the road and arrested within 15 minutes later. One man was injured and taken to hospital under a police escort.

The haul of 1.2 million cigarettes was confiscated on Mandelastraat in Delft on Friday. Earlier in the week police recovered 500,000 iillegal cigarettes in two vans in the town.

Officers are investigating whether the break-in at the police station is linked to the earlier raids in Delft.

World.title: Kaczyński appeals to President Nawrocki to unify Poland’s right-wing opposition ahead of elections
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Jarosław Kaczyński, the leader of Poland’s largest opposition party, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), has called on opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki to help unify the country’s various right-wing opposition forces ahead of next year’s parliamentary elections. His appeal comes as PiS, which for the last two decades has dominated the Polish right, is in crisis, amid falling polling numbers, a split by a breakaway faction, and a growing challenge from far-right parties that have long been critical of PiS. That has created a fragmented opposition, with parties competing against one another as much as or more than with the Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition. Some on the right hope that Nawrocki, who enjoys good relations with various parts of the opposition, could act as a unifying figurehead bridging those divides. 🔴 Jarosław Kaczyński ujawnił, o co osobiście poprosił Karola Nawrockiego. Podczas miesięcznicy smoleńskiej prezes PiS odniósł się do podziałów na prawicy i przyznał, że widzi dla prezydenta wyjątkowo ważną rolę: ma pomóc scalić zwaśnione środowiska. „Ja prezydenta swego czasu… pic.twitter.com/qwXhmccun2 — Super Express (@se_pl) August 10, 2026 Speaking on Sunday at a monthly commemoration of the 2010 Smolensk air disaster that killed his identical twin brother, then-President Lech Kaczyński, Jarosław was reported by a variety of Polish media outlets as saying that he had asked Nawrocki to act as a “patron” for a unified right. “I asked the president some time ago, and I hope he will do it,” said Kaczyński, quoted by newspaper Fakt. “It would be very good if the president took up this matter energetically.” “We could continue to develop – as we did during our years of government – not only in terms of achieving GDP growth, but also by undertaking major investments, by undertaking everything that would truly change Poland.” Kaczyński was referring to the period between 2015 and 2023 when a PiS-dominated coalition, known as the United Right (Zjednoczona Prawica), ruled Poland. In the latter year, it was ousted from power by a more liberal coalition led by Tusk, Kaczyński’s great rival. Since then, the landscape on the Polish right has changed dramatically. One of PiS’s partners in the United Right, the hard-right Sovereign Poland (Suwerenna Polska), merged with PiS in 2024. The other, the centre-right Agreement (Porozumienie), is now defunct. Meanwhile, support for PiS itself has collapsed. Having won 35% of the vote at the 2023 elections, it now averages only around 20% in polls – the party’s lowest figures for almost 20 years. To make matters worse, last month, around a fifth of the party’s MPs formed a breakaway group in parliament led by PiS deputy leader and former Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki. They plan to soon form their own, separate party, Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), with a more moderate, centre-right agenda than PiS. At the same time, PiS has found itself challenged by a growing far right. Confederation (Konfederacja), which won 7% of the vote in 2023, is now polling around 12-13%. The even more radical Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), which broke away from Confederation last year, is at 9%. The split in PiS is a blow to the party and its leader, Jarosław Kaczyński. But the potential emergence of a new centre-right party led by Mateusz Morawiecki could actually help the opposition win a majority at next year's elections, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/xMP7e4rOFf — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 31, 2026 That has resulted in a much more fragmented right, with four separate entities not only opposed to Tusk’s government but also competing with one another for overlapping electorates. With parliamentary elections scheduled for autumn 2027, there have been questions over whether and to what extent the opposition should seek to cooperate with one another. One option would be an agreement not to stand candidates against one another for seats in the upper-house Senate, which are contested on a single-member-district system rather than through the proportional representation that decides the share of seats in the more powerful lower-house Sejm. Parties in Tusk’s current ruling coalition themselves formed such a “Senate pact” at the 2019 elections, helping them win control of the upper house, then repeated that in 2023, when they retained control. Although the Senate has a limited legislative role, it would be a significant prize for Nawrocki and the opposition, especially if Tusk’s coalition wins the Sejm, because the Senate has the power to approve or reject national referendums proposed by the president. An even more ambitious plan that has been rumoured is for some elements of the right-wing opposition to run joint electoral lists for the Sejm. That would require a far greater degree of programmatic consensus and longer negotiations over how to distribute places on lists. The government's majority in the Senate has, for the second time, rejected a proposal by opposition-aligned President Nawrocki to hold a referendum on whether Poland should continue implementing the EU's climate policies, which he argues are too costly https://t.co/Idm6dnzQEH — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 6, 2026 Nawrocki is seen as key to any such plan coming to fruition. He was elected last year to the presidency as an independent, but with the formal backing of PiS. Ahead of the second-round run-off vote, he also received endorsements from defeated first-round rivals Sławomir Mentzen, one of the leaders of Confederation, and Grzegorz Braun, the leader of KKP. Since taking office, Nawrocki has continued to cultivate good relations with PiS and Confederation, as well as with Morawiecki’s new breakaway faction. However, he has kept his distance from Braun, whose anti-Americanism, antisemitism and sympathy towards Russia makes him something of a pariah. The European Parliament has again voted to strip Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun of immunity to face further charges for Holocaust denial as well as various antisemitic, anti-Ukrainian and anti-LGBT incidents during last year's presidential campaign https://t.co/4EHVEuSDnM — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 26, 2026 Media reports have suggested that Nawrocki is planning to play a role in creating a “broad patriotic camp” among the opposition ahead of next year’s elections. Last week, during an event celebrating the first anniversary of his swearing in, the president also hinted at this role. He noted he will, in the coming months, be presenting “a presidential development strategy”, which “I believe will become a point of reference in the upcoming parliamentary elections for all those who aspire to govern Poland, a real plan for the future of the republic”. The strategy would be aimed in particular at “patriotic forces” who are “ready for dialogue between the offices of the president and future prime minister”. Given that Nawrocki and Tusk’s government are bitterly opposed to one another, that was a clear reference to opposition parties. A report on Sunday by Newsweek Polska, based on unnamed inside sources, claimed that Kaczyński is hoping to form a single electoral list for the Sejm elections compromising PiS, Development Plus and all or parts of Confederation, under the patronage of Nawrocki. 💥 Nowa obsesja Jarosława Kaczyńskiego, w jaki sposób odzyskać władzę. Prezes PiS naciska na Karola Nawrockiego, by prezydent stworzył "listę Nawrockiego" prawicy do Sejmu. To najbardziej ryzykowna, ale też o ogromnej stawce, decyzja prezydenta.https://t.co/sqRPFUuiZ7 — Jacek Gądek (@JacekGadek) August 9, 2026 Other leaders on the right have expressed varying degrees of willingness to work with one another. Speaking to broadcaster TVN on Saturday, Krzystof Bosak, another of Confederation’s leaders, expressed support for the idea of a Senate pact. On Friday, Morawiecki said that he can “fully imagine working with Sławomir Mentzen”, who “I believe is absolutely part of the patriotic camp”. However, Mentzen himself quickly ruled out the idea, tweeting that he’d rather “quit politics than join this gang leading Poland to disaster”, adding that Tusk, Kaczyński and Morawiecki are “one and the same”. Whereas Bosak represents a nationalist faction of Confederation seen as more compatible with PiS, Mentzen represent’s a libertarian wing that is bitterly opposed to the former PiS’ government’s high social spending, support for Ukraine, and the restrictions it introduced during the COVID-19 pandemic. Prędzej mi ręka uschnie, niż poprę kolejne programy socjalne. Prędzej zrezygnuję z polityki, niż dołączę się do tej bandy prowadzącej Polskę do katastrofy. Tusk, Kaczyński, Morawiecki, Czarzasty, jeden pies. Dla nich wszystkich słupki sondażowe są ważniejsze od przyszłości… — Sławomir Mentzen (@SlawomirMentzen) August 7, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Protests against anti-Ukrainian violence held in 25 Polish cities
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Demonstrations took place in around 25 Polish cities on Sunday against a “growing wave of hate and violence” against Ukrainians, who are Poland’s largest immigrant group. The protests came after police data showed a significant increase in reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland so far this year, including a number of high-profile incidents of verbal and physical aggression. Sunday’s demonstrations, which took place under the slogan “Do Not Be Indifferent”, were organised by the Committee for the Defence of Democracy (KOD), an NGO, with support from other groups, including Amnesty International. “[This is] a nationwide campaign aimed at expressing opposition to the growing wave of hate, xenophobia, nationalism and violence directed against Ukrainians and members of other minorities,” wrote KOD ahead of the events. On Sunday, hundreds gathered on Warsaw’s Castle Square carrying Ukrainian and Polish flags and many waving signs saying “With U”, with the letter “U” coloured in Ukrainian national colours. #Siódemka Plac Zamkowy w Warszawie, protest w ramach: 🛑 NIE BĄDŹMY OBOJĘTNI! WSPÓLNIE PRZECIWKO NIENAWIŚCI! W wielu miastach Polski wyszliśmy na ulice, żeby jasno powiedzieć: nie ma zgody na hejt, przemoc i agresję wobec Ukraińców. W ostatnim czasie coraz częściej słyszymy… pic.twitter.com/kOfq4zBuGT — Piotr #FBPE Fijałkowski (@piotr4913) August 9, 2026 In Wrocław, Poland’s third-largest city, local media reported that around 150 people attended a demonstration, carrying placards saying “Let’s defend our neighbours from the aggression and stupidity of others” and “Putin is the enemy, Ukraine is our neighbour”. In Gdańsk, on Poland’s northern coast, around 300 people gathered, according to local media. However, they were also met with a small counter-demonstration of around a dozen people, led by the New Hope party that is part of Poland’s far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) opposition group. The counter-protesters held a banner declaring “Solidarity with victims of mass immigration” and “Down with Bandera”, a reference to historical Ukrainian nationalist leader Stepan Bandera, who in Poland is associated with the massacres of around 100,000 Poles by Ukrainians during World War Two. Separately, on Friday, a group of NGOs organised a demonstration against anti-Ukrainian violence outside the prime minister’s chancellery, during which they delivered a petition, signed by over 11,000 people, calling for the government to take “decisive action against xenophobic attacks”. Police data published last month showed that the number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland was 30% higher in the first half of this year compared to the same period in 2025. Among those incidents have been a number of high-profile cases, including two 11-year-old Ukrainian girls being verbally abused by a man on a bus in the city of Bielsko-Biała and a violent attack on young Ukrainians by a group of Polish teenagers in Warsaw. Ukrainians are by far Poland’s largest foreign national group, with around 1.6 million living in the country. While Poland welcomed Ukrainian refugees in 2022, there has been growing negative sentiment towards them recently, indicated in polls and through anti-Ukrainian rhetoric from prominent politicians. Tenions have been stoked further by a diplomatic crisis that began in May, when President Volodymyr Zelensky named a Ukrainian military unit after a group responsible for massacring Poles during World War Two. That prompted Polish President Karol Nawrocki to strip Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour. The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland is up 30% so far this year, police data show. The figures come following recent high-profile cases of verbal and physical attacks against Ukrainians, who are Poland's largest immigrant group https://t.co/pcTsJddDz7 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026 In particular, two far-right opposition parties, Confederation and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), have used anti-Ukrainian rhetoric, while the largest opposition group, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), has recently taken a tougher line towards Ukraine. Last week, PiS announced that, if it returns to power, one of its first actions would be to deport Ukrainian conscription-age men who are not in legal employment. At one of Sunday’s protests, in Kraków, a demonstrator responded with a placard declaring “Deport xenophobia”. Poland’s more liberal ruling coalition has condemned anti-Ukrainian rhetoric from the right-wing opposition. Last month, Prime Minister Donald Tusk called for a “war against this violence”, saying that “thugs and hooligans have gained courage, audacity and political patronage” from the opposition. Poland’s largest opposition party, the national-conservative PiS, has called for Ukrainian men of conscription age who are not legally working to be deported to Ukraine. The idea was criticised by the government, which called it "absurd" and "disgusting" https://t.co/Z4kArDeLXl — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 7, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Remains of Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in WWII exhumed in Ukraine
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The remains of a further 55 victims of massacres of Poles by Ukrainian nationalists during World War Two have been exhumed in Ukraine. Around half were children, and most show signs of brutal deaths, including skulls pierced with farming tools (as pictured above). The announcement comes amid ongoing tensions between Poland and Ukraine over the so-called Volhynia massacres, sparked by President Volodymyr Zelensky’s recent decision to name a military unit after the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), which was responsible for leading the killings of around 100,000 Poles. However, both sides have expressed hope that continued exhumations of victims – most of which are believed to still remain buried in unmarked mass graves in Ukraine – can ease that path towards reconciliation. 📣 Zakończenie tegorocznych prac ekshumacyjnych ofiar Zbrodni Wołyńskiej w Ostrówkach i Woli Ostrowieckiej ❗ Od 13 lipca do 7 sierpnia br. pracownicy Instytutu Pamięci Narodowej, przedsiębiorstwa „Wołyńskie Starożytności” oraz specjalista z zakresu medycyny sądowej z… pic.twitter.com/iDJR5NmdEn — Instytut Pamięci Narodowej (@ipngovpl) August 7, 2026 The new findings were made in Ostrówki and Wola Ostrowiecka, two neighbouring former villages, now depopulated, that were previously part of Poland but, after postwar border changes, are now located in western Ukraine. There, on 30 August 1943, the UPA massacred over 1,000 Poles and razed the villages to the ground. Similar massacres took place in many other villages, as part of an ethnic cleansing operation by the UPA to remove Poles and other minorities from what they saw as Ukrainian territory. Exhumations previously took place in Ostrówki and Wola Ostrowiecka in the 1990s, and again in 2011 and 2015, uncovering the remains of hundreds of victims. However, hundreds more are believed to remain buried. In 2017, Ukraine imposed a ban on searches for victims on its territory in response to the dismantlement of a monument to the UPA in Poland. However, in a diplomatic breakthrough last year, it allowed them to resume, including granting permission in December for work in Ostrówki and Wola Ostrowiecka. In April this year, mass graves were discovered there, with exhumations then beginning in July. Poland’s state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN) has now announced the result of that work. They have uncovered the remains of 55 victims, 26 of them children (mostly under 12 years of age, with the youngest a few months old) and 20 women. In the Volhynia massacres as a whole, the majority of victims were women and children. The locations and conditions of the remains reveal much about the manner of their death. Most were buried “at random” without coffins, which is consistent with contemporary accounts that they were killed in a barn and then thrown into a mass burial pit, notes the IPN Most of the remains, in particular skulls, show signs of injuries that are also consistent with contemporary accounts, which said that victims were ordered to lie on the ground before being killed with farm tools, including hammers for slaughtering cattle. Material from the bones has been secured for genetic testing, which was recently used for the first time to identify massacre victims exhumed at another location in Ukraine last year. Around 300 personal items, including rosaries, crosses and clothing, were also found during the recent excavations in Ostrówki and Wola Ostrowiecka. On 30 August, the 83rd anniversary of the massacre, the newly found remains will be buried in a funeral ceremony at the cemetery in Ostrówki. The IPN believes that over 300 further victims still remain buried at unknown locations in the two former villages. Poland has for the first time used DNA testing to identify the remains of Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in WWII. “After more than 80 years, families are receiving the answer they have awaited for generations,” says the culture minister https://t.co/c1gM3kQ83s — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 14, 2026 The Volhynia massacres have long been a point of tension between Poland, which recognises them as a genocide, and Ukraine, which rejects that label. The decision by Kyiv to allow exhumations to resume last year was regarded as a major step towards reconciliation. However, that process was undermined in May this year, when Zelensky decided to name a military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. That prompted an angry response from Warsaw, where President Karol Nawrocki stripped Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour. There have since been efforts to reach a diplomatic solution. Last month, Zelensky pointed specifically to the exhumation work in Ostrówki and Wola Ostrowiecka as evidence that “Ukraine is doing its part to fairly establish the facts about those who were killed in those years”. Subsequently, he announced a five-point plan to alleviate the crisis, including allowing more exhumations and opening up historical archives. Poland welcomed the move but said that it would wait to see how it was implemented in practice. Poland has cautiously welcomed President @ZelenskyyUa's announcement of a five-point plan to alleviate the diplomatic crisis triggered by his earlier decision to name a military unit after a group that led massacres of Poles during WWII https://t.co/M3GXD9vtAr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 18, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Candidate to lead Polish state history institute rejected in rare clash between houses of parliament
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. In a rare clash between Poland’s two houses of parliament, in both of which the government has a majority, the Senate has rejected a candidate chosen by the Sejm to become the new head of the state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN). The nominee, Mateusz Szpytma, has served as deputy head of the IPN since 2016, including when it was under the leadership of Karol Nawrocki, who last year was elected president of Poland with the support of the national-conservative opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party. Szpytma’s candidacy has been opposed by most of Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition, who argue he helped politicise the IPN under the former PiS government. However, some more conservative elements of the coalition joined the opposition in supporting Szpytma, giving him a majority in the Sejm but not the Senate. Senatorowie nie wyrazili zgody na powołanie Mateusza Szpytmy na Prezesa Instytutu Pamięci Narodowej – Komisji Ścigania Zbrodni przeciwko Narodowi Polskiemu — Senat RP 🇵🇱 (@PolskiSenat) August 6, 2026 The IPN is a body tasked with researching, documenting and educating about Poland’s tumultuous and tragic 20th-century history. It also has the power to prosecute crimes relating to the periods when the country was under Nazi and communist rule. The institute was led by Nawrocki from 2021 until August last year, when he became president of Poland. Since then, the IPN has been without a permanent head. Last October, the IPN’s council nominated Karol Polejowski, another of the institute’s deputy heads, to be its new president. But he was rejected by the Sejm, which, along with the Senate, must approve the choice. In April, the council instead recommended Szpytma, whose candidacy was approved by the Sejm last month. He received support mainly from opposition parties, including PiS and the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja). However, in a rare split within the ruling coalition, one of its junior members, the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), also backed Szpytma, as did some MPs from the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050). That was enough to give him a majority. By contrast, the main ruling party, Tusk’s Civic Coalition (KO), and The Left (Lewica) opposed his nomination, citing a letter signed earlier this year by 170 academics, who described Szpytma as “one of the faces of IPN’s politicisation” under the former PiS government. However, PSL’s leader, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, who also serves as Poland’s defence minister and deputy prime minister rejected that characterisation and said that PSL had backed Szpytma because of his work commemorating historical figures from the agrarian movement in which PSL is rooted. In a rare split in the ruling coalition, MPs from two parties, PSL and Poland 2050, voted with the opposition in the Sejm for a new head of the Institute of National Remembrance. However, PM Donald Tusk says their choice will be rejected by the Senate https://t.co/0CGmbsNp4F — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026 However, it was widely expected that Szpytma’s candidacy would be blocked by the upper-house Senate, where even the PSL and opposition combined do not have a majority in the 100-seat chamber. That was confirmed in a vote on Thursday, when 50 senators were opposed to Szyptma and only 38 were in favour, with one abstention. “We voted against further politicisation” of IPN and “against tolerating financial irregularities”, wrote the speaker of the Senate, Małgorzata Kidawa-Błonska of KO. The latter comment was likely a reference to a report by the Supreme Audit Office (NIK) last year which found that the IPN had, between 2022 and 2025, failed to properly manage tens of millions of zloty in spending, including various violations of regulations on the use of public funds. Szpytma told journalists that he was not surprised by the result of the vote, saying he believes his connection to Nawrocki, who is an ardent opponent of the current government and has vetoed a record number of laws, is the reason why he lost. Nie zgodziliśmy się w Senacie, by człowiek Karola Nawrockiego został prezesem IPN. Zagłosowaliśmy przeciw dalszemu upolitycznianiu Instytutu. Przeciw tolerowaniu nieprawidłowości finansowych. Pan Szpytma nie wprowadziłby żadnych zmian w funkcjonowaniu IPN. — Małgorzata Kidawa-Błońska (@M_K_Blonska) August 6, 2026 The IPN plays an important role in Polish public life, including in commemorating, investigating and prosecuting crimes that took place during the Nazi-German and Soviet occupations of Poland in World War Two, as well as during the decades of communist rule afterwards. Under Nawrocki’s leadership, the IPN accelerated the process of demolishing remaining Soviet monuments in Poland, often prompting criticism from Russia. It has also been closely involved in the exhumation of victims of the Volhynia massacres, in which Ukrainian nationalists killed around 100,000 Poles during World War Two. During PiS’s time in power from 2015 to 2023, the IPN was accused of becoming increasingly politicised, using its activities to support the historical narratived promoted by the government. In 2021, Israel protested after a former far-right activist was appointed to head one of the IPN’s local branches. Russia has criticised the "sacrilegious" demolition of a Soviet monument in Poland, calling it a “flagrant violation” of a bilateral agreement. But Poland's @ipngovpl says it was a "propaganda object" that had to be removed under a "decommunisation" law https://t.co/73T99ZlPqU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 4, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Polish state energy giant Orlen posts record half-year profit amid Middle East turmoil
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish state energy giant Orlen posted a record profit in the first half of 2026, as turmoil in the Middle East boosted earnings in the fuel sector, despite Polish government measures to cushion the rise in consumer prices. Orlen has also this year seen its highest ever proportion of revenue from foreign markets. The results come amid a political dispute over a government plan to impose a windfall tax on excess profits from fuel sales, aimed at recouping billions spent on consumer subsidies. Orlen would be the biggest target of the tax, but the plan has been obstructed by opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki. W pierwszym półroczu Orlen zarobił na czysto 15,8 miliarda złotych. Trzy razy więcej niż przed rokiem.https://t.co/qJS81csI0H — TVN24 BiS (@TVN24BiS) August 6, 2026 On Thursday, Orlen reported consolidated net profit of 15.9 billion zloty (€3.7 billion) for the first six months of the year, almost tripling from the 5.7 billion zloty recorded in the same period of 2025. Revenue rose to 152.2 billion zloty from 134.4 billion zloty. CEO Ireneusz Fąfara acknowledged that the figures came amid exceptional market conditions. Energy prices jumped globally in March, after the US and Israel began to attack Iran and Tehran responded by blocking the Strait of Hormuz, a key export route. Fąfara noted that, despite this, Poland had maintained some of Europe’s lowest fuel prices. He said that Orlen had prioritised fuel availability and competitive domestic prices while taking advantage of stronger margins abroad, where it brought in an “absolutely record level of revenue from foreign markets”. In the first half of 2026, foreign markets accounted for 35.7% of Orlen’s revenue, up from 33.8% a year earlier. The bulk came from Germany, the Czech Republic, Lithuania and Austria, where Orlen operates petrol stations, as well as from trading activities in markets such as the Netherlands and Switzerland. Pierwsze półrocze 2026 roku ORLEN zamyka rekordowym zyskiem z rynków zagranicznych. Wynik netto całej Grupy w II kwartale wyniósł 7,7 mld zł. Wypracowane wyniki finansowe pozwoliły na wypłatę rekordowej dywidendy dla akcjonariuszy oraz dalsze finansowanie największego programu… pic.twitter.com/ohcxksuv4G — ORLEN (@GrupaORLEN) August 6, 2026 Orlen has expanded rapidly in recent years, as it has swallowed up other state-owned energy firms and sought to diversify away from its traditional focus on oil towards gas, renewables and hydrogen. In March this year, Orlen’s market valuation rose to its highest ever level of €35.2 billion, up from €7 billion in early 2022. As a result, it overtook the market capitalisation of Russian energy giant Gazprom. Mateusz Czyżkowski, an analyst at brokerage XTB, attributed Orlen’s record profits this year to “skilful balancing between geopolitical conditions and local pressures”, including government-imposed fuel price caps that squeezed margins. “The global commodities market in the second quarter of 2026 was strongly buoyed by tensions between Iran and Israel and ongoing disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz…This significant geopolitical premium boosted profits in [Orlen’s] Upstream & Supply segment,” he wrote in a note. The announcement of record profits comes as Orlen finds itself at the centre of a political dispute over the government’s proposed windfall tax, which would introduce a 60% levy on excess profits from liquid fuel sales. The measure was expected to raise around 4 billion zloty, which would have offset most of the roughly 4.7 billion zloty the government spent on keeping fuel prices lower for consumers amid the crisis in the Middle East by, among other things, cutting VAT and introducing a maximum daily price. However, although the tax was approved by the government’s majority in parliament in July, President Nawrocki refused to sign it into law, instead referring it to the constitutional court for review – a process that has no time limit and can take years. President @NawrockiKn has obstructed a planned windfall tax on fuel companies by sending it to the constitutional court, where it could stay for years The tax aimed to offset fuel price protection costs after the Iran war surgehttps://t.co/UojVuYhvdV — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 27, 2026 According to government calculations, Orlen would account for around 60% of the tax base if the measures eventually come into force. However, at his press conference on Thursday, Fąfara emphasised that the company supports the windfall tax. “We have viewed this solution positively from the very beginning. I believe it is in the interest of the company, our customers, and the country,” he said. However, Fąfara rejected suggestions that Orlen could unilaterally reduce pump prices by sacrificing margins. “We cannot lower prices in defiance of the market and global prices…If we lowered prices below parity, there would be a shortage of fuel,” he warned, adding that artificially low prices would encourage speculative exports and fuel tourism. Prices at petrol stations jumped today in Poland after the government ended the last of the support measures introduced to cushion consumers from the energy crisis caused by the war in Iran. New Polish opposition group Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), which recently broke away from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party, has proposed the idea of paying a “parental salary” for the first three years of a child’s life. The idea is part of a package of proposals to tackle Poland’s dire demographic situation released on Friday by Development Plus in its first major policy announcement since leader Mateusz Morawiecki announced that the group would soon become a political party. 3600 zł miesięcznie na dziecko do 3. roku życia – jedna z wielu propozycji @RozwojPlus dla demografii! Pensja Rodzicielska wynosząca równowartość płacy minimalnej, czyli obecnie około 3600 zł netto miesięcznie przez pierwsze 3 lata życia dziecka. To ponad czterokrotnie więcej… pic.twitter.com/253pwcskNK — Mateusz Morawiecki (@MorawieckiM) August 7, 2026 The proposed parental salary would amount to 3,600 zloty (€837) per month, the equivalent of the minimum wage after taxes. It is 4.5 times more than the current child benefit payment of 800 zloty per month that all Polish parents of children under 18 receive. Development Plus says that the parental salary could be combined with income from other work that parents undertake and that it would include contributions towards their pensions. It would end once a child turns three, after which parents would have access to normal child benefit payments. The group says that, for now, the idea is just a proposal, based on expert analysis of how to tackle Poland’s demographic crisis, and that it now wants to “refine it through dialogue with Poles” rather than “imposing top-down provisions”. Poland has long been grappling with a shrinking, ageing population. Last year, the number of births fell to a new post-war low of 238,000, while deaths totalled 406,000. That marked the 13th consecutive year in which more people died than were born in Poland. The country’s fertility rate – meaning the average number of children that are born to a woman over her lifetime – fell to a new record low of 1.068 in 2025. That is one of the lowest figures anywhere in the world and well below the so-called “replacement rate” – the figure needed to ensure that the population does not decline – which is generally defined as 2.1. Poland’s fertility rate, already one of the lowest in the world, fell to a new record low of 1.07 in 2025, deepening concerns over the country's shrinking and ageing population https://t.co/OMGC1MpA5l — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 28, 2026 Successive Polish governments have introduced various measures intended to boost the birth rate, though so far without clear success. The former PiS government, with Morawiecki as finance minister and later prime minister, introduced and expanded the current child benefit programme. While there was a brief bump in births after it was launched in 2016, numbers subsequently continued their downward trend. After PiS lost power in 2023, the current government, led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, continued the child benefit programme and also introduced new payments to support parents who return to work and restored funding for IVF treatment, which was previously cut by PiS. When announcing the proposed parental salary on Friday, Development Plus also outlined seven other proposed new policies to ease Poland’s demographic problems. One would allow workers to have a portion of their contributions go towards their parents’ pensions. Another pledged to provide better maternity care, including access to anaesthesia, a private hospital room and dedicated midwife, prenatal testing, and infertility treatment. Other policies promised more flexible working arrangements and mortgage repayments to prevent people from having to choose between a family or a career, as well as school hours and after-school care that “adapt to the lives of families, not the other way around”. Development Plus also proposed “granting parents the right to represent the voices of their minor children”. However, they provided no details of what this would mean in practice. Dzieci to nasza przyszłość! To fundament bezpieczeństwa Polski i polska racja stanu. Jak sprawić, by Polaków rodziło się coraz więcej? Oto strategia demograficzna dla Polski Stowarzyszenia @RozwojPlus🇵🇱➕. pic.twitter.com/1hiQPNuL47 — Mateusz Morawiecki (@MorawieckiM) August 7, 2026 Development Plus was founded as an association by Morawiecki in April this year. That immediately prompted criticism from some other members of the party, who saw it as a step towards creating a breakaway group. Matters came to a head last month, when PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński demanded that all the party’s lawmakers sign a pledge of loyalty and commit to leave any political associations they are part of. Morawiecki and his allies refused to do so, prompting Kaczyński to declare that meant they had effectively resigned from the party. Last week, Development Plus announced it had formed its own separate parliamentary caucus with 40 MPs in the Sejm, the most powerful lower house of parliament. The move immediately made it the third-largest group in the parliament, while also meaning PiS was no longer the biggest. On Monday this week, Morawiecki confirmed that his group would soon form a party of its own. He laid out a vision of a more moderate, centre-right party that would focus on economic development rather than “ideological disputes”, following PiS’s shift in a more hardline direction over recent months. Poland’s largest opposition party, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), has called for Ukrainian men of conscription age who are not legally working to be deported to Ukraine. The policy, which continues a recent hardening of PiS’s position towards Ukraine and Ukrainians as it competes with the far right for support, was condemned by government figures, who called it “absurd” and “disgusting”. 🇵🇱 Bezpieczeństwo obywateli powinno być priorytetem każdego rządu. Potrzebne są zdecydowane działania wobec osób przebywających w Polsce niezgodnie z prawem. 👉 Udostępnij! 🔥 Ku nowemu rządowi! pic.twitter.com/m8MctmmPXd — Prawo i Sprawiedliwość (@pisorgpl) August 6, 2026 On Thursday, PiS, which has recently been hit by falling support in the polls and the defection of a large breakaway group of more moderate MPs, held a policy convention at which it presented ideas it wants to implement if it returns to power after next year’s parliamentary elections. “One of [our] government’s first, most significant decisions will be to deport men, Ukrainians of military age, who are not legally working in Poland,” announced Tobiasz Bocheński, a deputy leader of the party. “They will have the opportunity to fight for their homeland, so that the horrors of this war can quickly end,” he continued. “Because for Central and Eastern Europe to be secure and free, Ukraine must win.” Bocheński denied that the policy was inhumane, noting that, in 2022, when PiS was in government, “Poles, like no other nation in Europe, opened their hearts, their homes and their wallets to women, children, the elderly and disabled people fleeing Putin’s bombs”. Poland was the primary destination for refugees fleeing Ukraine in 2022. Almost one million of them remain in the country, alongside hundreds of thousands of other Ukrainian immigrants, many of whom arrived before 2022. They are by far Poland’s largest foreign national group. In their announcement of the proposed policy, PiS gave no details of how it would work in practice, nor on what legal basis Ukrainians who are legally resident in Poland and have not violated any laws would be deported. News website Interia, which had reported on PiS’s plans shortly before they were officially announced, notes that data from Poland’s labour ministry show that only around 11,000 Ukrainians are registered as unemployed in Poland. The figures are not broken down by gender, but most are believed to be women. However, PiS’s policy would also apply to Ukrainians in the so-called grey economy, where people work informally without registering or paying taxes, reports Interia. Military-age Ukrainian men in other European countries should not receive social benefits, says Poland's foreign minister, @sikorskiradek. "There should be no financial incentives for avoiding the draft" https://t.co/5TcTqyDa6X — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 16, 2024 PiS’s plan was immediately criticised by government figures, with interior ministry spokeswoman Karolina Gałecka calling it “an absurd idea” and “pure demagoguery”. She noted that over 95% of Ukrainian men of conscription age in Poland are working legally and paying taxes. “Without these people, many key sectors of the Polish economy would simply grind to a halt,” wrote Gałecka. “Stop the incitement.” Deputy interior minister Maciej Duszczyk, meanwhile, told broadcaster TVN that, among the Ukrainian men not working, many are wounded soldiers in Poland for treatment and rehabilitation or fathers caring for disabled children. Deportations are a “purely political, disgusting idea”, he added. Interior minister Marcin Kierwiński wrote that, “when [PiS] was in power, they couldn’t even deport those who were breaking the law, and now they’re supposedly going to deport everyone without rhyme or reason”. Since taking power, the current government has increased deportations of foreigners who are in Poland illegally or broke the law while in the country. Last year, it carried out over 9,000 deportations, up from 7,200 in 2023, the last year that PiS was in power Absurdalny pomysł @pisorgpl ws. deportacji Ukraińców to czysta demagogia! Ponad 95% mężczyzn w wieku poborowym legalnie pracuje w 🇵🇱 i płaci podatki (dane ZUS).@OficjalnyJK zapowiada deportacje. A jak miałoby to wyglądać w praktyce? Patrole sprawdzające dokumenty na ulicach?… — Karolina Gałecka (@K_Galecka) August 6, 2026 During the conference on Thursday, PiS emphasised its tough approach to migration more broadly, saying that it would “create a new, restrictive system for foreigners” that would track each immigrant in the country. “Every foreigner will have their own individual account,” and if they commit any offences or fail to abide by any administrative obligations, “the information will be immediately entered into the system, and the deportation process will begin”, said Bocheński. “The only good migration is the return of Poles from abroad,” declared the party on social media. 🛡️ Bezpieczne granice to bezpieczna Polska. Skuteczna ochrona granic i walka z nielegalną imigracją to obowiązek każdego odpowiedzialnego państwa. 👉 Udostępnij! 🔥 Ku nowemu rządowi! pic.twitter.com/rRPZpmXi5U — Prawo i Sprawiedliwość (@pisorgpl) August 6, 2026 In fact, it was during PiS’s time in power from 2015 to 2023 that Poland saw the largest wave of immigration in its history, and one of the largest anywhere in Europe. In every year between 2017 and 2022, Poland was the EU member state that issued the highest number of first residence permits to immigrants from outside the bloc. There are now over two million foreigners registered as living in Poland, making up just 5% of the population. Around three quarters are Ukrainians (1.55 million), with the next largest groups being Belarusians (139,300), Indians (26,100), Georgians (22,200), Russians (19,500), Vietnamese (15,100) and Turks (14,500). The number of foreigners with residence permits in Poland has reached two million, making up just over 5% of the country’s population, new government data show. The largest national group by far are Ukrainians, followed by Belarusians and Indians https://t.co/SI09WtR7hR — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 26, 2026 While in government, PiS welcomed Ukrainian migrants and refugees and was a strong supporter of Ukraine in its defence against Russian aggression. However, since going into opposition, it has taken an increasingly tough line. That has reflected a broader shift in Polish society, with a variety of polls showing rising negative sentiment towards Ukraine and Ukrainians. Recent months have also seen a rise in reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland, including a number of high-profile incidents. Meanwhile, two far-right parties that have long taken an anti-Ukrainian stance, Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), have soared in the polls, placing pressure on PiS to toughen its own position. One Confederation MEP, Stanisław Tyszka, mocked PiS’s latest policy announcement. “PiS wants to heroically deport hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians whom they themselves let into Poland,” he wrote. “Comedy.” The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland is up 30% so far this year, police data show. World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Poland’s power grid operator, PSE, has, for the second time in three days and third time this summer, invoked emergency measures to ensure supply amid an ongoing heatwave. Before this summer, it had only done so twice in the eight years since such powers were introduced. However, following a meeting with PSE and other state energy officials, Prime Minister Donald Tusk has assured Poles that, despite “a very difficult period”, the “situation is under control” and power supplies are secure, thanks in part to the growth of renewables in recent years. ❗️PSE ponownie ogłaszają okresy przywołania na rynku mocy❗️ To już 3. raz w tym roku, kiedy operator sięga po to narzędzie. W historii zdarzyło się to tylko 5 razy, wliczywszy 3 przypadki tegoroczne, co pokazuje wyjątkowość roku 2026 dla energetyki. pic.twitter.com/DbCPnpyae4 — Jakub Wiech (@jakubwiech) August 6, 2026 PSE has called on contracted electricity generators to increase output and large consumers to cut use to help balance the grid on Thursday between 5:00 p.m. and 10:00 p.m., as temperatures have this week approached 40°C (104°F) in many parts of the country. The same measures were introduced on Tuesday, as the heatwave pushed up electricity consumption, partly due to increased use of air conditioning and refrigeration. Participants in Poland’s capacity market are paid for maintaining standby capacity and fulfilling their obligations when called upon by the operator. According to PSE, the mechanism is “a remedial measure” used when the generation capacity available to the operator falls significantly below the required safety level. Previously, the measures were invoked in June this year, amid another heatwave that saw Poland hit its highest-ever recorded temperature of 40.5°C. But before that, they had only been used twice since being introduced in 2018. Temperatures in Poland have reached the highest level on record, with a figure of 40.3°C (104.5°F) recorded this afternoon, as the heatwave that has hit Europe this week moves eastwards https://t.co/eRhRxiuCGq — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 28, 2026 Poland’s weather institute IMGW issued heat warnings on Thursday for 13 of the country’s 16 provinces, with daytime temperatures forecast to reach between 33C and 38C. High temperatures and prolonged drought conditions have also pushed water levels in many rivers to extremely low levels, with the Vistula, Poland’s longest river, only 5 centimetres above the historic low of 4 centimetres it fell to in Warsaw last year. Some other parts of the river have hit all-time record lows, reports Polsat News. One result has been a disruption of cooling supplies to Poland’s power sector. State energy firm Enea this week announced reduced operations at two of its coal-fired plants that are cooled by water from the Vistula. Around 1.1 gigawatts (GW) of capacity (just over 1% of Poland’s total) has gone offline. On Wednesday, Prime Minister Donald Tusk convened a meeting of a government crisis team, including PSE’s deputy president, to discuss the current heatwave and its potential impact on the power sector. However, afterwards he assured that “the situation is under control” and that the fact that Poland now has “a lot of energy from solar panels and wind turbines makes our system relatively secure”, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Poland’s renewable sector has expanded rapidly over the last decade. Last year, it provided just over 29% of the country’s power, with onshore wind supplying 14% of the energy mix and solar 12%. Renewables generated 29.4% of Poland's electricity in 2025, almost exactly the same figure as in 2024, ending a period of strong growth since 2021. Coal (52.2%) remained the dominant source, though its share declined.
