World.title: Alan Jones trial live updates: Court hears brother of complainant ‘J’ received gifts from 2GB broadcaster as alleged indecent assault, sexual touching trial continues
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of day six of Alan Jones’ lengthy criminal trial on charges of indecent assault and sexual touching. Our reporters Clare Sibthorpe and Jacqueline Maley will be bringing you the latest from the courtroom today.

Last week, the NSW Local Court in Sydney’s historic Downing Centre court complex heard allegations that Jones indecently assaulted a young athlete, starting with unwanted kissing when the man was a teenager in year 12 in the early 2000s. Jones denies the claims.

Alan Jones outside the Downing Centre Local Court on Tuesday. Sam Mooy

Our live coverage was paused on Wednesday after Local Court Judge Glenn Walsh temporarily imposed a non-publication order on the cross-examination of the complainant, known as “J”, by Jones’ barrister, Gabrielle Bashir, SC. That order was lifted on Thursday afternoon.

“J”, now in his early 40s, denied under questioning by Bashir that he had a financial motive for making the allegations against Jones, and denied that they were a fabrication.

He has given evidence that Jones groped him as he drove the then-radio host to his Fitzroy Falls farm. “J” has also told the court that Jones had indecently assaulted him at the property after telling him to wear “a robe and nothing else”.

The complainant said he came forward to police after seeing reports about Jones’ arrest in November 2024 because he wanted justice.

Jones had supported the promising athlete financially, including paying him hundreds of dollars a week to focus on training and giving him a car and a mobile phone, the court heard.

Today, the man known as complainant “J” returns to the witness box for a sixth day. He will be re-examined by prosecutor Georgina Wright, SC, after his cross-examination concluded on Friday.

A man known as “C” will be the next complainant to give evidence.

Bashir asked “J” a series of questions about whether he read media reports containing similar allegations about Jones in 2023 before he spoke to police the following year. He said he did not.

The Crown alleges that Jones indecently assaulted or sexually touched six men between 2003 and 2020, and is seeking to prove 22 charges against him, including nine indecent assault charges against “J”.

The former broadcaster has emphatically denied wrongdoing, and Bashir said during her opening address to the court that the credibility and reliability of the complainants’ evidence would be tested.

“Rivalry, treachery, double-dealing, money, hatred, desperation, opportunism and more are all at the heart of this case,” Bashir said in her opening remarks to the court.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

World.title: The new brand of hate radicalising Australian teens
World.content:
Australia’s counter-terrorism chief has warned of a rise in youth radicalisation fuelled by online extremism, as he raised alarm about the spread of harmful rhetoric from foreign “propaganda machines” and social media platforms with no regard for content moderation. Experts appearing before the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion on Tuesday warned “nihilistic violent extremism” was pushing young people to pursue violence for its own sake as government responses to radicalisation came under the microscope. Counter-terror coordinator Brendan Dowling warned of a rise in youth radicalisation fuelled by online extremism. The Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion Brendan Dowling, who was named counter-terrorism coordinator at the Department of Home Affairs in May, sounded the alarm on nihilistic extremism as an emerging driver of terror that glorifies violence and is absent of a structured ideology. It differed from previous iterations of terrorism by promoting violence itself, rather than considering it a method to advance an ideology or cause, Dowling said.



The trend has intensified the work of tackling mixed and unclear ideologies through counter-terror circles, as new trends of radical behaviour flourish in online environments. “There is a lot of evolution, a lot of fluidity, and it is something that I think even long-standing experts would appreciate that you’re never on top of,” he told the commission. “There’s always a continued process of learning.” Youth Justice NSW senior manager Steve Barracosa said extremism has evolved beyond religious or ideological boundaries. Royal Commission into Antisemitism and Social Cohesion Youth Justice NSW specialist support unit senior manager Steve Barracosa told the hearing extremist themes can intersect in “quite incoherent ways”. “Nihilistic violent extremism has become a bit of a catch-cry for misanthropic, violent, gore, objectionable spaces online where meshed ideas are mixing together,” he said.



Barracosa said youth extremism programs have expanded since 2022 as the problem evolved beyond religious and ideologically fuelled radicalisation with the emergence of “a really broad and convoluted right-wing extremism landscape with many different themes and ideas”. Related Article Antisemitism royal commission Push to train imams in Australia, warning of Islamophobia spike “We’ve observed antisemitic narratives, ideas, and in some cases ideologies across different pockets of the extremism landscape, particularly religious and right-wing extremism,” he said. But antisemitism was seldom the core defining feature or most prominent theme of a radicalised young person’s extreme beliefs. “We’re living in a rather complex, divisive, provocative, and emotive socio-political climate, which I think must be incredibly difficult for younger, increasingly vulnerable cohorts to navigate,” Barracosa said.



He warned young people are more susceptible to “short, sharp, very intense radicalisation trajectories” that can occur online. Naveed Akram and father Sajid Akram are accused of conducting the Bondi Beach massacre in December after being radicalised by IS propaganda. Their car was adorned with an IS flag, and they allegedly recorded a video manifesto containing the terror group’s iconography. The younger Akram survived and is awaiting trial on murder and terrorism charges. Sajid was shot and killed during the attack. Online networks and communication methods are creating more ways for radical material to spread. Matt Davidson Dowling flagged a “disturbing” uptick in young Australians being swept up by online extremist material promoting neo-Nazi, white supremacist, Jihadi and anti-government movements, saying that the spread of harmful rhetoric online meant “effectively anyone” could engage with radical ideology.



“Your average Australian … might have a sort of stereotype in their head of what an extremist or a terrorist looks like, or how they behave ... we’re seeing such [a] greater variance in types of people engaging with radical ideas,” he told the commission. Australia’s counter-terror authorities found that online material, seeking to legitimise ideological grievances and justify acts of violence, is “nearly always” driving radicalisation, according to Dowling. “In nearly all cases there is an online dimension where [there is] access to violent extremist material online, access to a community of like-minded people, who foment that sense of grievance and anger,” he said. Related Article Antisemitism royal commission Police ‘gave control of CBD’ to Opera House protesters, royal commission hears Dowling pointed to hateful rhetoric spread by voice on gaming platforms during live sessions. He also took aim at social media operators, accusing them of not doing “as much as they can” to stop violent content spreading, and foreign actors “trying to fuel that sense of grievance”.



“The Russian government globally operates propaganda machines, bot campaigns that try to identify divisive topics, extremist topics, and fuel those because they see that as part of their geostrategic agenda,” said Dowling, who also singled out Iran and its proxies “potentially” engaging in similar work. “When you see material that is promoted and available online because of its level of views or its virality that is not necessarily natural or organic … that is, I think, an increasing area of concern for us.” Corrective Services NSW assistant commissioner Danielle Matsuo told the hearing of the importance of early intervention in combating extremism. “By the time people come to us, they often have very entrenched views and beliefs,” he said. Forming new habits, behaviours and “new ways of navigating the world” is central to custodial de-radicalisation programs, Matsuo said.



Efforts to disengage young people from radical ideas depend heavily on their own willingness, family engagement and care provision, but Barracosa said intense intervention needs to be sustained to be successful. “Short gains are positive, but the maintenance of those gains requires service providers to remain involved with any given young person over a prolonged period,” Barracosa said. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Albanese, Taylor hammer out deals on gambling and tech, but ignore Howard’s last-ditch plea
World.content:
PoliticsFederalOnline gambling Albanese, Taylor hammer out deals on gambling and tech, but ignore Howard’s last-ditch plea Paul Sakkal Updated August 11, 2026 — 3:47pm ,first published August 10, 2026 — 10:20am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Opposition Leader Angus Taylor are hammering out deals on charging tech giants for news, cutting the NDIS, and curbing betting promotions, prompting the Coalition to mull a broader bargain on tax and migration. A last-minute plea from former prime minister John Howard to go further on sports betting s appears unlikely to sway the leaders, who excluded the Greens to do a rare Labor-Coalition deal on a set of thorny issues as One Nation eats into their vote. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, former prime minister John Howard and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese. Alex Ellinghausen, Dylan Coker Resisting pressure from Labor and Liberal backbenchers and Howard to go further on gambling, Albanese insisted he had got the balance right between acknowledging those who “have a punt on a Saturday” and protecting kids and addicts, pitching his day of deal-making as delivering “outcomes over outrage”. “We choose a different road: we choose progress over protest,” he told Labor MPs in Canberra, after this masthead reported worry in cabinet over One Nation portraying a full ban on betting ads as a nanny-state solution.



“We choose unity over division … We’re here to make a difference.” Albanese is expected to yield from his positions by restricting betting inducements and reversing a change to the News Bargaining Incentive that large media outlets said would crimp their revenue. Both were aimed at winning Taylor’s support and satisfying corporate demands, clearing the path for a clutch of legislative wins in the first parliamentary session after the winter break. Powerful media and sporting stakeholders were worried about the Greens’ more strident positions on policies where Albanese was keen to bank quick wins. Photo: Matt Golding Coalition sources involved in the talks with Labor said the party would now think about how it could leverage its in-principle agreement to move quickly on the NDIS. The opposition may demand speedy resolution of a quirk in Labor’s negative gearing laws that hurts widows or seek a commitment to give the Coalition some wins on its upcoming migration overhaul, which One Nation has sought to exploit. As politicians returned to Canberra on Monday after the winter break, one of Albanese’s first items of businesses was scheduling a meeting with Taylor to salvage his big tech agenda from the brink of defeat and to win support for plans to force US platforms to pay for news and block gambling advertising.



Sources on both sides said that Albanese and Taylor had a detailed discussion on betting ads. The long-running policy debate has pitted gambling harm advocates against big media firms, including this masthead’s owner Nine, and sports. Albanese and Taylor agreed to work on amendments that would strengthen restrictions on inducements, a week after bombshell allegations that betting firms were holding drug-fuelled events with big gamblers. Labor has initially resisted going further on inducements. Country Racing Victoria chief executive Scott Whiteman said cash-strapped regional racing would be “up the creek” financially if it could not reward punters with free bets and other “generosities”. Taylor and Albanese face off in parliament earlier this year. Alex Ellinghausen Howard made a last-ditch plea for Albanese and Taylor to take on powerful media and sports outfits by cracking down hard on sports betting ads. The former leader rubbished Labor’s proposed opt-out system which relies on people telling a social media platform or broadcaster they do not want to see ads, telling this masthead it was “against human nature to expect people to sit down and opt out”. Instead, Howard declared it would be “far better” to create a new opt-in system whereby people would be shielded from promotions unless they volunteered to see them. The opt-in model is supported by the Greens and some major party MPs, but the major party cabinets view the idea as too extreme.



“I think it should be the attitude of all the major political parties, both Labor and Coalition, to legislate in the public interest. And if that means disappointing major companies, then disappoint them,” Howard said in an interview. “It’s a very poor thing that young people grow up thinking that gambling on sport is a normal part of life.” Taylor told reporters in Canberra: “We’ve seen three years of delay from Labor on dealing with this but … we will work with the government to make sure it is right.” Loading Albanese and Taylor also held looser discussions on the NDIS, which the Coalition delayed but was always likely to eventually support, and the News Bargaining Incentive. The NDIS changes, which could pass the Senate next week, would shift 160,000 people away from the bulging system and save up to $38 billion over four years. Every month in which the laws were not tightened would cost the budget about $1.5 billion.



A week after the largest news firms pleaded with the prime minister to reverse last-minute changes to the News Bargaining Incentive, Albanese also expressed optimism about settling on a model to push Meta, Google and TikTok to pay for news articles. The tech giants argue there is no justification for the policy because news outlets benefit from distributing their work on social media. Related Article Media & marketing News Corp says plan to make tech giants pay for news has been ‘gutted’ Albanese has pledged to stand up for the scheme in the face of threats from the Trump administration, which has described the tech taxes as extortion. The news scheme was at risk of collapse after Nine and News Corp savaged amendments that may have lowered payments to big media outlets and pushed money to smaller ones. The news bargaining incentive is a world-first framework to draw revenue from tech giants to fund journalism.



The key change that infuriated the news organisations would hypothetically reduce any one firm’s portion of the fund from $25 million to less than $17 million. The change was made by Labor without consultation. It was designed to benefit smaller publishers, but large outlets argued it undervalued the bigger players who hire the most journalists. World.title: RBA keeps rates on hold as major bank warns of 15% property price slump
World.content:
The Reserve Bank has kept interest rates on hold as it weighs a slowing economy, dragged down by a weaker-than-expected housing market, against risks that inflation could be pushed up by an “AI boom” and continued conflict in the Middle East. On Tuesday the bank kept the official cash rate at 4.35 per cent – broadly in line with economists’ expectations – after releasing its updated forecasts for key metrics including economic growth, inflation and unemployment. Financial markets believe there is a 50-50 chance of a further rate rise late in the year, with rate relief not expected before the second half of 2027. House prices are falling in Labor’s marginal Melbourne seats but local MPs say community supports it. Joe Armao The decision comes after ANZ economists on Tuesday morning warned that property prices could slump by almost 15 per cent over this year and next, citing interest rates, low levels of affordability and the federal government’s property tax changes. In its monetary policy decision statement the RBA said the decision to keep interest rates on hold was unanimous, and that the board remained focused on ensuring high inflation did not become embedded.



“Following three increases in the cash-rate target since the beginning of the year, financial conditions are now tighter than they were, and the economy appears to be slowing as expected,” the board said. “But inflation is still too high.” The board said “inflation is likely to remain high for some time” due to the disruption to global oil supply caused by the US and Israel’s war against Iran, with higher fuel prices being passed through to other goods and services. The bank said it expected economic growth to be slightly stronger for the rest of the year than it thought back in May, although it noted the figure was likely to remain below the long-run rate of 2 per cent. Its forecasts show growth of 1.4 per cent by Christmas and 1.6 per cent by December next year. Price growth across the economy remains above the RBA’s target range of 2 to 3 per cent – inflation was 3.8 per cent in June – but the inflation figures were substantially lower than the 4.8 per cent figure the RBA forecast in May.



The RBA said household consumption has eased “gradually”, with spending on discretionary items including electric vehicles remaining relatively strong. Meanwhile, business investment had been much stronger than expected, the bank said, largely driven by data centre construction. Editor's pick Census Completing the census is compulsory. Skipping it can result in a hefty fine Unemployment, at 4.4 per cent in June, is still below the rate the bank considers “full employment”: the level at which it believes inflation pressures will not be stoked as people look for more work in response to cost-of-living pressures. Treasurer Jim Chalmers has said the Reserve Bank’s decision to keep interest rates steady would “come as a relief to Australians with a mortgage”. “This decision reflects the fact that inflation has been coming in well under the Reserve Bank and Treasury forecasts,” Chalmers said in parliament.



Meanwhile, ANZ, which had been the most bearish about the property market of all the major banks, said it believed capital city prices would fall by 4.3 per cent this year and by 3.4 per cent in 2027 before staging a recovery the following year. Combined, the falls would mean a drop of 10.6 per cent from the peak in prices to their trough. The biggest hit is expected in Sydney, where the median value is now $1.5 million, with house prices tipped to fall by 14.5 per cent from their peak at the start of the year. Melbourne prices are tipped to fall by 12.8 per cent from their peak. Loading Prices in both cities are expected to recover by almost 5 per cent in 2028.



Smaller hits are expected in other capitals, with drops of 7.9 per cent forecast in Brisbane, 5.2 per cent in Perth and 9.8 per cent in Adelaide. In these three cities prices have climbed by more than 15 per cent over the past two years. ANZ senior economists Madeline Dunk and Adam Boyton said the market was slowing quicker than they had expected. Related Article Exclusive

Property prices Teal MPs’ electorates are where house values are falling most. They think it’s a good thing “It is clear the combination of restrictive interest rates, recent tax policy changes and global uncertainty have dampened sentiment in the market,” they said. “Auction clearance rates are very soft, coming in below 50 per cent for the past 10 weeks across the capitals.”



Dunk and Boyton said interest-rate settings, and ongoing pressures on the construction sector, meant prices were unlikely to fall for too long. They are tipping a nationwide increase of 4.3 per cent in 2028. “Given the broader supply backdrop, and the capacity constraints in the construction sector, we think it is hard to see housing prices falling for an extended period,” they said. “Through the second half of 2027 we expect dwelling prices to start recovering, supported by 50 basis points of rate cuts from the RBA.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: What apology over Rinehart skit tells us about Hugh Marks’ ABC. It’s not good
World.content:
CultureTV & radioABC Opinion What apology over Rinehart skit tells us about Hugh Marks’ ABC. It’s not good Jenna Price Columnist August 11, 2026 — 3:41pm

August 11, 2026 — 3:41pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Can we please give this kid a break? I’m talking Kate McGuinness, the runner-up in the ABC’s Race Around the World. She is currently on the receiving end of a massive bollocking from Gina Rinehart and her acolytes. Don’t know the backstory? A handful of extremely precocious filmmakers killed themselves for months to win the golden ticket – a chance to make a half-hour documentary for the ABC. Look, even with Hugh Marks in charge (and chair Kim Williams lurking over his shoulder), it’s still an amazing opportunity. Filmmaker Kate McGuinness in her controversial Race Around the World film. ABC Those of us who saw the first iteration of this hyperreality show 20-odd years ago remember it so vividly. We also remember John Safran, whose fearless satirical take-downs of religion made him a national star. How weird that we now think it’s even worse to disrespect money than it is to disrespect religion. Now, one of those contestants was Kate McGuinness. She poked fun at mining magnate Rinehart. I mean, what she said and did was not funny in any way, shape or form. I don’t have a great sense of humour myself. For example, I watch what passes for comedy and nothing ever happens. But I did run it past a few funsters in my life, and they didn’t think it was funny either.



But the reaction was out of control. Completely out of control. And that’s because Gina Rinehart has the entire right-wing media at her beck and call. She’s probs got Rupert allocated to the family chat. Aren’t we horrified that an overwhelmingly powerful, wealthy woman is bullying someone less than half her age? All hell broke loose, assisted by the hounds of Holt Street and the strays at Southbank. They’ve always hated the ABC, so this gave them even more fodder. Wonder why News Corp hates the national broadcaster? Always about money. The ABC gives away for free what News struggles to get people to pay for. ABC managing director Hugh Marks. Dominic Lorrimer Let’s get this out of the way. McGuinness’ comments about Rinehart weren’t any good. Silly. But the idea that she was trying to encourage violence is absolute rubbish. She’s a comedian trying to be funny. Good on her. With comedy as in life, it’s OK to fail and keep trying. Producers could have been more of a guiding hand, but I reckon the ABC is struggling with mentoring at the minute. I just don’t recall any of these folks getting particularly worked up about “ditch the witch”. It’s always OK to try to prick hugely inflated egos and status bubbles. We should always be about decapitating tall poppies. (Fortunately for me, at 149 centimetres and shrinking, I’ve only ever been a short poppy.)



What happened to the country I grew up in, joyfully poking fun at rich and powerful people? Are we now so frightened of status and influence that we don’t back the upstart? Sure, McGuinness wasn’t, ah, courteous, but why do we think that matters? Shall I give you a list of those who are neither tasteful nor polite? We would be here all day, because it would be a very long list. It is not the job of a comedian to be tasteful or polite. That is not the point. The point is to be funny and McGuinness will keep working on that so long as she isn’t bullied from her life’s work by Rinehart’s mates. If McGuinness could get to work on that racist member of the globalist elite, Pauline Hanson, that would be glorious. Related Article Exit Interview

Australian TV ‘Hate on my colleagues’: The brutal feedback Race Around the World contestants faced McGuinness is 29! (What I didn’t know at 29 would fill entire data centres). She’s on a very big stage, and she’s still on her L plates. Not tasteful? Geez, when I was her age, I made a three-part radio documentary on sex during menstruation, broadcast on community radio. Despite complaints to whatever ACMA was called back in the day, my station manager Keith Jackson, now retired in Noosa, backed me. And Hugh Marks? Glad he’s not my boss. What a suck-up to News Corp.



Just a reminder, Mr Marks. There are parts of News Corp that are promoting the globalist agenda of Pauline Hanson, the politician who won’t let the ABC into news conferences. Hanson, who is Rinehart’s buddy. Hanson, who is promoting the idea of defunding the ABC. Don’t cosy up to these people. It won’t work to protect you. What’s happening to Kate McGuinness is a pile-on and the ABC has folded like a concertina fan. The National Portrait Gallery had more gonads when it refused to buckle to Rinehart’s pressure to remove her portraits by Western Aranda artist Vincent Namatjira. The job of our cultural institutions is not to accept the billionaire view of the world, where might and money are always right. I asked Matthew Ricketson, co-author with Andrew Dodd of Getting Murdoched: How Murdoch’s Media Wields Power and Punishment*, now being reprinted, what he thought of the attacks on McGuinness. He described it as a classic News pile-on. Free speech is fine until you don’t agree with it. “Whatever the original offence was is far outweighed by the pile-on,” he said. “This is part of a sustained campaign to kick the ABC in the head.” Rinehart is doing her utmost to destroy McGuinness because the zillionaire’s feelings are hurt. She’s not a politician, but she’s trying to back one. We should all resist her and everyone who stands with her. And right now, that includes Hugh Marks.



* I’ve been a target of News and was interviewed for Getting Murdoched. Hey, Kate, trust me. You will survive. Jenna Price is a regular columnist.

World.title: It’s not just Gina Rinehart who failed to make a killing on SpaceX
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesElon Musk Opinion It’s not just Gina Rinehart who failed to make a killing on SpaceX Elizabeth Knight Business columnist August 11, 2026 — 3:32pm

August 11, 2026 — 3:32pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There are more than 28,000 Australian retail shareholders nursing a SpaceX sentiment sag – albeit they are in good company alongside our country’s richest person, Gina Rinehart. After Australia’s retail investors were given special permission (via prospectus additions) to buy directly into this blockbuster US float of Elon Musk’s rocket business in June, it was an irresistible punt for a cohort well known for their love of betting. For Rinehart, investing $1.4 billion of her fortune into SpaceX reflected her well-established Musk fan-girl credentials. It’s a big number, even if she can afford to lose some of it. But for the other 28,000-plus Australian mum and dad punters, there hasn’t been much joy or excitement in the financial return on their investment. The SpaceX IPO had a huge take-up of retail investors which made Elon Musk the world’s first trillionaire. Getty Images



After being the most hyped float of all time, the shares have spent half their public market life below the issue price. The only big winners were those that sold in the first week. This week the SpaceX share price has picked up a bit and now sits close to its issue price of $US135 ($191), so owners of the stock are no longer wearing an uncomfortable loss. It’s certainly better than last week’s low of $US104.83. But the buzz around this company was so noisy that retail investors were looking for a big payday. Retail investors didn’t punt on SpaceX just to get their money back. Last Friday marked a pivot point in trading when retail investors globally turned from net buyers to net sellers, according to tracking data from Vanda Research. There could be many reasons for this but reassessing the reward against the risk would be one.



Related Article Opinion

Sharemarket Burning billions: SpaceX’s sales are soaring, but its spending even more so Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Vanda estimates that retail traders on average paid $US147 for SpaceX shares since the initial public offering. It also cites evidence that retail investors had been actively buying the stock when it dipped. This average retail buy-in price is well below the current price, so the many sellers are simply cutting their losses. SpaceX is the ultimate casino-type bet. There are experts ascribing a value for SpaceX shares of $US800 and others who say it’s worth no more than $US100.



In only two months since its listing, the shares have moved between $US225 and $US104 – with little company news being reported, other than last week’s earnings report. The good news is that the company reported revenue that was generally higher than analysts were expecting, and management’s revenue forecasts were bullish. This should have provided some comfort to retail investors that underneath all that hot-air hype, the actual business was making decent strides. Gina Rinehart, a SpaceX investor, has praised the business and its founder Elon Musk. The bad news is that nothing in those performance numbers would support the nosebleed share prices at which SpaceX traded in the first couple of weeks after its float. In addition, the high proportion of big investors betting the stock price will fall (as much as one-third of the stock on issue has been sold “short”) is a headwind to share-price performance.



The release last week of almost 1 billion shares (held by staff and early investors) meant more SpaceX shares were added to the tally of those eligible to trade. That (over)supply shock was absorbed relatively well but it is the first of several releases of stock. Related Article Opinion

Sharemarket Is SpaceX a meme stock? Elon Musk loses trillionaire status Kishor Napier-Raman Senior Business Writer Each of the additions to the supply of stock will curb the scarcity value that helped push shares into the stratosphere in the first week following its debut. Now that the three-ring circus of the SpaceX listing has packed up, all investors will need to adjust to the reality that SpaceX shares will move in tandem with the market’s moveable appetite for risk. When US President Donald Trump’s war rhetoric towards Iran is toned down, or when the Federal Reserve makes dovish comments on US interest rates, SpaceX shares (and plenty of other risky shares) will respond positively.



But at moments when investors succumb to a bout of AI fear, SpaceX shares will catch a bout of that negative sentiment. Investors will also be watching whether management’s optimistic near-term revenue targets will be reached, rather than tracking Musk’s ambitions for earthlings to populate Mars. World.title: 230 in one boat: Migrants are piling onto mega-dinghies to get to UK
World.content:
WorldEuropeRefugees 230 in one boat: Migrants are piling onto mega-dinghies to get to UK Nick Gutteridge , Max Stephens , Vivian Song and Charles Hymas August 11, 2026 — 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

France’s lifeboat service has warned there is “no limit” to the number of migrants people-smugglers will put on a boat to Britain. The French national sea rescue service (SNSM) warned it was seeing “more and more” large boats ferrying hundreds of migrants across the Channel. A ‘mega-dinghy’ in action ferrying refugees across the English Channel from France. SNSM On Monday morning (UK time) a record 230 asylum seekers arrived in Britain after travelling on a single 15-metre-long vessel from near Berck-sur-Mer, Normandy. The vessel, which was intercepted by Border Force, HM Coastguard and the Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI), surpassed the previous record of 165 migrants who reached the UK in a single boat in July.



Jean-Marc Lamblin, the director of the SNSM’s Berck-sur-Mer branch, said: “Over the past three months we’ve been seeing more and more 15-metre boats passing through.” He added that when the 150-migrants-per-boat figure was recently surpassed, “we didn’t think there could be any more, but there really is no limit now”. Many of the “mega-dinghies” used for Channel crossings are manufactured in China, then shipped via commercial routes through countries such as Turkey and Bulgaria to European staging posts, chiefly Germany. International smuggling networks store and distribute them at the staging posts before they reach the French beaches from where they are launched. Home Office officials have previously identified Chinese websites as a key source of boats and parts, and have been working with Beijing to clamp down on them. A source at the National Crime Agency said China was “likely to be one of the countries but not the only country” from which smuggling gangs obtained their equipment.



Related Article Analysis

Immigration How the storming of Ceuta shifts Europe to the right It was not clear whether the mega-dinghy used in Monday’s crossing came from China. UK government sources said smuggling gangs were turning to such large vessels out of desperation to make the crossings financially viable. Last week people-smugglers packed 173 people onto a boat attempting to cross the Channel but they were returned to France after its engine caught fire. Joint operations between the British and French police on the ground have meant more planned launches are thwarted early, while co-operation with countries including Germany and China has helped restrict their supply of boats and engines.



French police are deploying new tactics to counter the growing use of mega-dinghies, including targeting and dispersing large gatherings of migrants near the coast, which are often a sign that a launch is imminent. As a result, the gangs were finding it increasingly difficult to launch enough small boats to make ends meet, officials said, meaning they were having to turn to cramming large numbers of migrants onto single-vessel voyages instead. Many of the “mega-dinghies” used for Channel crossings are manufactured in China and then shipped to European staging posts, chiefly Germany. SNSM A government source told The Telegraph: “Sustained pressure from law enforcement means the gangs are finding it harder to launch boats, and are therefore being forced to place more people onto them. “While this boat is larger, the number of crossings is down significantly, and we just had the lowest figures for a July since 2020.”



Officials said overall numbers of migrants arriving were down by 43 per cent compared with the previous year. This was despite the fact that August is one of the busiest periods of the year for “red days”, when sea conditions are most suitable for crossing. The average number of migrants per small boat has increased from seven in 2018 to 63 in the year to March, and 70 so far this month. But they warned that the smugglers’ use of larger boats had made both the crossings and the rescue operations at sea more perilous. The SNSM said about 30 people had ended up in the sea during the rush to climb on the mega-dinghy at about 5pm on Sunday. Some became cut off by the tide and needed to be rescued. French lifeboat workers noted that the large dinghy was first seen with about 50 migrants on board, then cruised close to a beach, picking up more people. The crowded dinghy was described as “buckling under the swell” as it headed towards Britain.



Dr Mihnea Cuibus, senior researcher at the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford, said: “There has been a longstanding trend of smugglers fitting increasingly more migrants onto larger and more crowded boats. “It is likely that this is at least partly driven by increased enforcement in and around the French coast. Related Article Immigration ‘Impenetrable border’: Farage claims Australian plan can stop the boats to Britain “Authorities have been trying to make it harder for smugglers to obtain boats, disrupting supply chains and confiscating equipment alongside European partners and thus creating incentives to fit as many people as possible into available boats.” The average number of migrants per small boat has increased from seven in 2018 to 63 in the year to March, and 70 so far this month.



Nigel Farage, the leader of Reform UK, said the record-breaking crossing proved the “illegal invasion is a national security emergency”. In a post on X he said: “At 2.30am this morning, a boat carrying 230 people was taken into Dover. This is a record number in a single vessel. It’s yet more proof that this illegal invasion is a national security emergency.” The boats are getting bigger as smuggling gangs look to make the crossings financially viable. Getty Images Chris Philp, the shadow home secretary, said the French authorities should have stopped the dinghy. He said: “This is now beyond a joke. The French authorities could easily have stopped a vessel this size from embarking in shallow waters. “I recently saw for myself French gendarmes standing by and doing nothing while illegal immigrants boarded in knee-deep water. Shabana Mahmood is handing over £660 million of our money while this happens. It’s a disgrace.”



Related Article Immigration People in this city want the boats to stop. But they haven’t met Rishan A spokesman for Europol, the EU’s law enforcement agency, said: “The European Centre Against Migrant Smuggling is aware of this development. “We are in constant exchange with the appropriate authorities in both France and the United Kingdom on this phenomenon and also have a dedicated operational taskforce running that concentrates on smuggling of migrants with boats (no matter if relatively small boats or, as of recently, larger boats) across the Channel.” A Home Office spokesman said: “This latest incident demonstrates the reckless and dangerous tactics employed by the criminal gangs facilitating these crossings, who continue to put lives at risk by cramming ever greater numbers of people onto unseaworthy vessels. “We are making progress, with the number of small boat crossings down this year and the lowest number recorded for the month of July since 2020.



“But we must go further, which is why we have signed a payment-by-results deal with the French to put 40 per cent more boots on the ground on French beaches.” The Telegraph, London Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: At least 132 people killed, many trapped as powerful earthquake hits Colombia
World.content:
Updated WorldSouth AmericaEarthquakes At least 132 people killed, many trapped as powerful earthquake hits Colombia Astrid Suarez , Megan Janetsky and Juan Diaz Updated August 11, 2026 — 4:07pm ,first published August 11, 2026 — 2:32am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Bogota, Colombia: A powerful 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck western Colombia, killing at least 132 people, destroying a hospital, damaging hundreds of buildings and leaving many trapped under debris while their loved ones and rescue workers searched through rubble. Many of the deaths were concentrated in the city of Pereira, in Colombia’s western coffee-growing region, with surrounding cities and the Valle del Cauca region also hit hard, the BBC reported. Loading More than 480 people were injured in the quakes, Colombia’s Association of Capital Cities wrote in a statement, and the death toll is likely to rise, with many people reportedly trapped under the rubble. Colombia’s President Abelardo de Espriella, who was inaugurated only on Friday, has declared a state of emergency and pledged to personally oversee the emergency response.



“We aren’t going to leave people alone. They are in our hearts, and we are going to tend to people with our full determination,” he said. Volunteers help shift debris at a collapsed building in the city Pereira, which was close to the quake’s epicentre. Getty Images The president gave an initial estimate that about 1600 buildings had been damaged, including some 61 which had completely collapsed. The quake struck at 7.34am on Monday (10.34pm AEST) at a depth of 103 kilometres. Its epicentre was in San Jose Del Palmar, a community of about 4800 people in the Choco region about 400 kilometres west of the capital Bogota, the US Geological Survey said. A vehicle is crushed by debris after the earthquake struck Cali, Colombia, on Monday. AP Photo/Juan Diaz



The quake ravaged other cities across western Colombia, including Quibdo, Cali and Manizales, and was also felt in neighbouring Ecuador and Panama, though minimal damage was reported there. In Cali, the country’s third-largest city, search teams and civilians picked through the remains of destroyed buildings, passing large pieces of concrete and other rubble down a long line of volunteers. Residents and rescue workers in Cali search through the rubble. AP Photo/Santiago Saldarriaga The desperate scene brought memories of the searches still ongoing in neighbouring Venezuela weeks after that country was devastated by two powerful earthquakes. Colombia’s Geological Service said the earthquake was the strongest recorded in Colombia “in the 21st century”, and that it was followed by 21 less powerful aftershocks.



While Colombia typically registers thousands of small quakes every month, Northwestern University seismologist Suzan van der Lee said the strong magnitude, an inland epicentre near soft river valleys and plate movement may have contributed to more intense damage. View post on X “This one was far below the [Earth’s] crust, and in theory, it shouldn’t cause as much shaking. At this magnitude, it did actually cause a lot of shaking,” she said. “A magnitude 7.4 is about 32 times as powerful as a magnitude 6.4.” Colombia’s Pacific region around the quake’s epicentre lies along the “Ring of Fire”, the line of seismic faults encircling the Pacific Ocean where most of the world’s earthquakes occur. The Pacific, particularly the Choco region, is one of the poorest regions in the country. Nestled in the dense jungle, much of Choco is only reachable by boat or plane, which may pose a problem for authorities in assessing the wider toll.



Jorge Moncayo, a 64-year-old taxi driver in Cali, said he saw plumes of dust shoot up across the city as buildings collapsed. Residents and rescue workers were searching the rubble for survivors. “My entire house shook. I’ve never lived through such a powerful earthquake,” he said. “We’re thanking God we’re alive.” The rescue effort in Cali. AP Photo/Santiago Saldarriaga Local authorities said the death toll included at least 40 people who were killed in the Risaralda region, where the hard-hit city of Pereira is located, as well as 27 people in the Valle del Cauca region, where Cali is located, including three children. Authorities also confirmed nine people killed in Choco, two in the Caldas region and a 73-year-old in the Antioquia region. It was not immediately clear where the other 32 people died.



The New York Times quoted the region’s governor, Dilian Francisca, saying that one hospital had collapsed, another had been overwhelmed with victims and that patients had been evacuated from a third hospital. Authorities said flights were suspended at the airports of Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago, Buenaventura and Pereira as they assessed damage. The earthquakes left many in the Andean nation unnerved after two back-to-back quakes devastated neighbouring Venezuela in late June, destroyed hundreds of buildings and killed more than 5000 people. Little was known about the extent of the damage in Choco, a remote region where officials reported dozens of injured people and damaged buildings, but few other details. Phone signals were out in many parts of the region’s capital, Quibdo. The town closest to the earthquake’s epicentre, San Jose del Palmar, has no airport and is located on top of a mountain ridge along a highway linking the cities of Cali and Pereira.



In Pereira, photos and videos published by local media showed pieces of the airport ceiling falling on people taking shelter, who were screaming. In the city, people were shown running through rubble and plumes of dust. Pereira Mayor, Mauricio Salazar, told a local radio station that more people were trapped under “a massive quantity of collapsed buildings”. A rescue worker searches for survivors. Santiago Saldarriaga In nearby Manizales, one of the towers of the neo-Gothic cathedral collapsed and fell on the nave. Mayor Jorge Eduardo Rojas asked residents to stay outside in case of aftershocks. Police look at a building damaged after an earthquake struck Colombia. AP Photo/Vladimir Encima



In Cali, a city of 2 million people, Mayor Alejandro Eder said that residents were trapped in at least 19 buildings that had collapsed. Small earthquakes, known as “temblores”, are common in central and western Colombia, but those with magnitudes higher than 6.0 are rare. In 1999, a 6.2-magnitude quake near the city of Armenia killed more than 1100 people. Patients evacuated from a hospital in Cali. Santiago Saldarriaga The earthquake presents the first major challenge to De la Espriella, a Trump ally who was only sworn in as president over the weekend. Messages of support have rolled in from other leaders in the region, including Mexico, Brazil, Ecuador, El Salvador and the United States. “The Trump administration is closely monitoring the large earthquake that struck Colombia and stands ready to support the people of Colombia,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio wrote in a post on X.

World.title: Alan Jones trial live updates: Court hears brother of complainant ‘J’ received gifts from 2GB broadcaster as alleged indecent assault, sexual touching trial continues
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of day six of Alan Jones’ lengthy criminal trial on charges of indecent assault and sexual touching. Our reporters Clare Sibthorpe and Jacqueline Maley will be bringing you the latest from the courtroom today.

Last week, the NSW Local Court in Sydney’s historic Downing Centre court complex heard allegations that Jones indecently assaulted a young athlete, starting with unwanted kissing when the man was a teenager in year 12 in the early 2000s. Jones denies the claims.

Alan Jones outside the Downing Centre Local Court on Tuesday. Sam Mooy

Our live coverage was paused on Wednesday after Local Court Judge Glenn Walsh temporarily imposed a non-publication order on the cross-examination of the complainant, known as “J”, by Jones’ barrister, Gabrielle Bashir, SC. That order was lifted on Thursday afternoon.

“J”, now in his early 40s, denied under questioning by Bashir that he had a financial motive for making the allegations against Jones, and denied that they were a fabrication.

He has given evidence that Jones groped him as he drove the then-radio host to his Fitzroy Falls farm. “J” has also told the court that Jones had indecently assaulted him at the property after telling him to wear “a robe and nothing else”.

The complainant said he came forward to police after seeing reports about Jones’ arrest in November 2024 because he wanted justice.

Jones had supported the promising athlete financially, including paying him hundreds of dollars a week to focus on training and giving him a car and a mobile phone, the court heard.

Today, the man known as complainant “J” returns to the witness box for a sixth day. He will be re-examined by prosecutor Georgina Wright, SC, after his cross-examination concluded on Friday.

A man known as “C” will be the next complainant to give evidence.

Bashir asked “J” a series of questions about whether he read media reports containing similar allegations about Jones in 2023 before he spoke to police the following year. He said he did not.

The Crown alleges that Jones indecently assaulted or sexually touched six men between 2003 and 2020, and is seeking to prove 22 charges against him, including nine indecent assault charges against “J”.

The former broadcaster has emphatically denied wrongdoing, and Bashir said during her opening address to the court that the credibility and reliability of the complainants’ evidence would be tested.

“Rivalry, treachery, double-dealing, money, hatred, desperation, opportunism and more are all at the heart of this case,” Bashir said in her opening remarks to the court.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

World.title: The new brand of hate radicalising Australian teens
World.content:
Australia’s counter-terrorism chief has warned of a rise in youth radicalisation fuelled by online extremism, as he raised alarm about the spread of harmful rhetoric from foreign “propaganda machines” and social media platforms with no regard for content moderation. Experts appearing before the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion on Tuesday warned “nihilistic violent extremism” was pushing young people to pursue violence for its own sake as government responses to radicalisation came under the microscope. Counter-terror coordinator Brendan Dowling warned of a rise in youth radicalisation fuelled by online extremism. The Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion Brendan Dowling, who was named counter-terrorism coordinator at the Department of Home Affairs in May, sounded the alarm on nihilistic extremism as an emerging driver of terror that glorifies violence and is absent of a structured ideology. It differed from previous iterations of terrorism by promoting violence itself, rather than considering it a method to advance an ideology or cause, Dowling said.



The trend has intensified the work of tackling mixed and unclear ideologies through counter-terror circles, as new trends of radical behaviour flourish in online environments. “There is a lot of evolution, a lot of fluidity, and it is something that I think even long-standing experts would appreciate that you’re never on top of,” he told the commission. “There’s always a continued process of learning.” Youth Justice NSW senior manager Steve Barracosa said extremism has evolved beyond religious or ideological boundaries. Royal Commission into Antisemitism and Social Cohesion Youth Justice NSW specialist support unit senior manager Steve Barracosa told the hearing extremist themes can intersect in “quite incoherent ways”. “Nihilistic violent extremism has become a bit of a catch-cry for misanthropic, violent, gore, objectionable spaces online where meshed ideas are mixing together,” he said.



Barracosa said youth extremism programs have expanded since 2022 as the problem evolved beyond religious and ideologically fuelled radicalisation with the emergence of “a really broad and convoluted right-wing extremism landscape with many different themes and ideas”. Related Article Antisemitism royal commission Push to train imams in Australia, warning of Islamophobia spike “We’ve observed antisemitic narratives, ideas, and in some cases ideologies across different pockets of the extremism landscape, particularly religious and right-wing extremism,” he said. But antisemitism was seldom the core defining feature or most prominent theme of a radicalised young person’s extreme beliefs. “We’re living in a rather complex, divisive, provocative, and emotive socio-political climate, which I think must be incredibly difficult for younger, increasingly vulnerable cohorts to navigate,” Barracosa said.



He warned young people are more susceptible to “short, sharp, very intense radicalisation trajectories” that can occur online. Naveed Akram and father Sajid Akram are accused of conducting the Bondi Beach massacre in December after being radicalised by IS propaganda. Their car was adorned with an IS flag, and they allegedly recorded a video manifesto containing the terror group’s iconography. The younger Akram survived and is awaiting trial on murder and terrorism charges. Sajid was shot and killed during the attack. Online networks and communication methods are creating more ways for radical material to spread. Matt Davidson Dowling flagged a “disturbing” uptick in young Australians being swept up by online extremist material promoting neo-Nazi, white supremacist, Jihadi and anti-government movements, saying that the spread of harmful rhetoric online meant “effectively anyone” could engage with radical ideology.



“Your average Australian … might have a sort of stereotype in their head of what an extremist or a terrorist looks like, or how they behave ... we’re seeing such [a] greater variance in types of people engaging with radical ideas,” he told the commission. Australia’s counter-terror authorities found that online material, seeking to legitimise ideological grievances and justify acts of violence, is “nearly always” driving radicalisation, according to Dowling. “In nearly all cases there is an online dimension where [there is] access to violent extremist material online, access to a community of like-minded people, who foment that sense of grievance and anger,” he said. Related Article Antisemitism royal commission Police ‘gave control of CBD’ to Opera House protesters, royal commission hears Dowling pointed to hateful rhetoric spread by voice on gaming platforms during live sessions. He also took aim at social media operators, accusing them of not doing “as much as they can” to stop violent content spreading, and foreign actors “trying to fuel that sense of grievance”.



“The Russian government globally operates propaganda machines, bot campaigns that try to identify divisive topics, extremist topics, and fuel those because they see that as part of their geostrategic agenda,” said Dowling, who also singled out Iran and its proxies “potentially” engaging in similar work. “When you see material that is promoted and available online because of its level of views or its virality that is not necessarily natural or organic … that is, I think, an increasing area of concern for us.” Corrective Services NSW assistant commissioner Danielle Matsuo told the hearing of the importance of early intervention in combating extremism. “By the time people come to us, they often have very entrenched views and beliefs,” he said. Forming new habits, behaviours and “new ways of navigating the world” is central to custodial de-radicalisation programs, Matsuo said.



Efforts to disengage young people from radical ideas depend heavily on their own willingness, family engagement and care provision, but Barracosa said intense intervention needs to be sustained to be successful. “Short gains are positive, but the maintenance of those gains requires service providers to remain involved with any given young person over a prolonged period,” Barracosa said. World.title: Albanese, Taylor hammer out deals on gambling and tech, but ignore Howard’s last-ditch plea
World.content:
PoliticsFederalOnline gambling Albanese, Taylor hammer out deals on gambling and tech, but ignore Howard’s last-ditch plea Paul Sakkal Updated August 11, 2026 — 3:47pm ,first published August 10, 2026 — 10:20am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Opposition Leader Angus Taylor are hammering out deals on charging tech giants for news, cutting the NDIS, and curbing betting promotions, prompting the Coalition to mull a broader bargain on tax and migration. A last-minute plea from former prime minister John Howard to go further on sports betting s appears unlikely to sway the leaders, who excluded the Greens to do a rare Labor-Coalition deal on a set of thorny issues as One Nation eats into their vote. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, former prime minister John Howard and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese. Alex Ellinghausen, Dylan Coker Resisting pressure from Labor and Liberal backbenchers and Howard to go further on gambling, Albanese insisted he had got the balance right between acknowledging those who “have a punt on a Saturday” and protecting kids and addicts, pitching his day of deal-making as delivering “outcomes over outrage”. “We choose a different road: we choose progress over protest,” he told Labor MPs in Canberra, after this masthead reported worry in cabinet over One Nation portraying a full ban on betting ads as a nanny-state solution.



“We choose unity over division … We’re here to make a difference.” Albanese is expected to yield from his positions by restricting betting inducements and reversing a change to the News Bargaining Incentive that large media outlets said would crimp their revenue. Both were aimed at winning Taylor’s support and satisfying corporate demands, clearing the path for a clutch of legislative wins in the first parliamentary session after the winter break. Powerful media and sporting stakeholders were worried about the Greens’ more strident positions on policies where Albanese was keen to bank quick wins. Photo: Matt Golding Coalition sources involved in the talks with Labor said the party would now think about how it could leverage its in-principle agreement to move quickly on the NDIS. The opposition may demand speedy resolution of a quirk in Labor’s negative gearing laws that hurts widows or seek a commitment to give the Coalition some wins on its upcoming migration overhaul, which One Nation has sought to exploit. As politicians returned to Canberra on Monday after the winter break, one of Albanese’s first items of businesses was scheduling a meeting with Taylor to salvage his big tech agenda from the brink of defeat and to win support for plans to force US platforms to pay for news and block gambling advertising.



Sources on both sides said that Albanese and Taylor had a detailed discussion on betting ads. The long-running policy debate has pitted gambling harm advocates against big media firms, including this masthead’s owner Nine, and sports. Albanese and Taylor agreed to work on amendments that would strengthen restrictions on inducements, a week after bombshell allegations that betting firms were holding drug-fuelled events with big gamblers. Labor has initially resisted going further on inducements. Country Racing Victoria chief executive Scott Whiteman said cash-strapped regional racing would be “up the creek” financially if it could not reward punters with free bets and other “generosities”. Taylor and Albanese face off in parliament earlier this year. Alex Ellinghausen Howard made a last-ditch plea for Albanese and Taylor to take on powerful media and sports outfits by cracking down hard on sports betting ads. The former leader rubbished Labor’s proposed opt-out system which relies on people telling a social media platform or broadcaster they do not want to see ads, telling this masthead it was “against human nature to expect people to sit down and opt out”. Instead, Howard declared it would be “far better” to create a new opt-in system whereby people would be shielded from promotions unless they volunteered to see them. The opt-in model is supported by the Greens and some major party MPs, but the major party cabinets view the idea as too extreme.



“I think it should be the attitude of all the major political parties, both Labor and Coalition, to legislate in the public interest. And if that means disappointing major companies, then disappoint them,” Howard said in an interview. “It’s a very poor thing that young people grow up thinking that gambling on sport is a normal part of life.” Taylor told reporters in Canberra: “We’ve seen three years of delay from Labor on dealing with this but … we will work with the government to make sure it is right.” Loading Albanese and Taylor also held looser discussions on the NDIS, which the Coalition delayed but was always likely to eventually support, and the News Bargaining Incentive. The NDIS changes, which could pass the Senate next week, would shift 160,000 people away from the bulging system and save up to $38 billion over four years. Every month in which the laws were not tightened would cost the budget about $1.5 billion.



A week after the largest news firms pleaded with the prime minister to reverse last-minute changes to the News Bargaining Incentive, Albanese also expressed optimism about settling on a model to push Meta, Google and TikTok to pay for news articles. The tech giants argue there is no justification for the policy because news outlets benefit from distributing their work on social media. Related Article Media & marketing News Corp says plan to make tech giants pay for news has been ‘gutted’ Albanese has pledged to stand up for the scheme in the face of threats from the Trump administration, which has described the tech taxes as extortion. The news scheme was at risk of collapse after Nine and News Corp savaged amendments that may have lowered payments to big media outlets and pushed money to smaller ones. The news bargaining incentive is a world-first framework to draw revenue from tech giants to fund journalism.



The key change that infuriated the news organisations would hypothetically reduce any one firm’s portion of the fund from $25 million to less than $17 million. The change was made by Labor without consultation. It was designed to benefit smaller publishers, but large outlets argued it undervalued the bigger players who hire the most journalists. World.title: RBA keeps rates on hold as major bank warns of 15% property price slump
World.content:
The Reserve Bank has kept interest rates on hold as it weighs a slowing economy, dragged down by a weaker-than-expected housing market, against risks that inflation could be pushed up by an “AI boom” and continued conflict in the Middle East. On Tuesday the bank kept the official cash rate at 4.35 per cent – broadly in line with economists’ expectations – after releasing its updated forecasts for key metrics including economic growth, inflation and unemployment. Financial markets believe there is a 50-50 chance of a further rate rise late in the year, with rate relief not expected before the second half of 2027. House prices are falling in Labor’s marginal Melbourne seats but local MPs say community supports it. Joe Armao The decision comes after ANZ economists on Tuesday morning warned that property prices could slump by almost 15 per cent over this year and next, citing interest rates, low levels of affordability and the federal government’s property tax changes. In its monetary policy decision statement the RBA said the decision to keep interest rates on hold was unanimous, and that the board remained focused on ensuring high inflation did not become embedded.



“Following three increases in the cash-rate target since the beginning of the year, financial conditions are now tighter than they were, and the economy appears to be slowing as expected,” the board said. “But inflation is still too high.” The board said “inflation is likely to remain high for some time” due to the disruption to global oil supply caused by the US and Israel’s war against Iran, with higher fuel prices being passed through to other goods and services. The bank said it expected economic growth to be slightly stronger for the rest of the year than it thought back in May, although it noted the figure was likely to remain below the long-run rate of 2 per cent. Its forecasts show growth of 1.4 per cent by Christmas and 1.6 per cent by December next year. Price growth across the economy remains above the RBA’s target range of 2 to 3 per cent – inflation was 3.8 per cent in June – but the inflation figures were substantially lower than the 4.8 per cent figure the RBA forecast in May.



The RBA said household consumption has eased “gradually”, with spending on discretionary items including electric vehicles remaining relatively strong. Meanwhile, business investment had been much stronger than expected, the bank said, largely driven by data centre construction. Editor's pick Census Completing the census is compulsory. Skipping it can result in a hefty fine Unemployment, at 4.4 per cent in June, is still below the rate the bank considers “full employment”: the level at which it believes inflation pressures will not be stoked as people look for more work in response to cost-of-living pressures. Treasurer Jim Chalmers has said the Reserve Bank’s decision to keep interest rates steady would “come as a relief to Australians with a mortgage”. “This decision reflects the fact that inflation has been coming in well under the Reserve Bank and Treasury forecasts,” Chalmers said in parliament.



Meanwhile, ANZ, which had been the most bearish about the property market of all the major banks, said it believed capital city prices would fall by 4.3 per cent this year and by 3.4 per cent in 2027 before staging a recovery the following year. Combined, the falls would mean a drop of 10.6 per cent from the peak in prices to their trough. The biggest hit is expected in Sydney, where the median value is now $1.5 million, with house prices tipped to fall by 14.5 per cent from their peak at the start of the year. Melbourne prices are tipped to fall by 12.8 per cent from their peak. Loading Prices in both cities are expected to recover by almost 5 per cent in 2028.



Smaller hits are expected in other capitals, with drops of 7.9 per cent forecast in Brisbane, 5.2 per cent in Perth and 9.8 per cent in Adelaide. In these three cities prices have climbed by more than 15 per cent over the past two years. ANZ senior economists Madeline Dunk and Adam Boyton said the market was slowing quicker than they had expected. Related Article Exclusive

Property prices Teal MPs’ electorates are where house values are falling most. They think it’s a good thing “It is clear the combination of restrictive interest rates, recent tax policy changes and global uncertainty have dampened sentiment in the market,” they said. “Auction clearance rates are very soft, coming in below 50 per cent for the past 10 weeks across the capitals.”



Dunk and Boyton said interest-rate settings, and ongoing pressures on the construction sector, meant prices were unlikely to fall for too long. They are tipping a nationwide increase of 4.3 per cent in 2028. “Given the broader supply backdrop, and the capacity constraints in the construction sector, we think it is hard to see housing prices falling for an extended period,” they said. “Through the second half of 2027 we expect dwelling prices to start recovering, supported by 50 basis points of rate cuts from the RBA.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: What apology over Rinehart skit tells us about Hugh Marks’ ABC. It’s not good
World.content:
CultureTV & radioABC Opinion What apology over Rinehart skit tells us about Hugh Marks’ ABC. It’s not good Jenna Price Columnist August 11, 2026 — 3:41pm

August 11, 2026 — 3:41pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Can we please give this kid a break? I’m talking Kate McGuinness, the runner-up in the ABC’s Race Around the World. She is currently on the receiving end of a massive bollocking from Gina Rinehart and her acolytes. Don’t know the backstory? A handful of extremely precocious filmmakers killed themselves for months to win the golden ticket – a chance to make a half-hour documentary for the ABC. Look, even with Hugh Marks in charge (and chair Kim Williams lurking over his shoulder), it’s still an amazing opportunity. Filmmaker Kate McGuinness in her controversial Race Around the World film. ABC Those of us who saw the first iteration of this hyperreality show 20-odd years ago remember it so vividly. We also remember John Safran, whose fearless satirical take-downs of religion made him a national star. How weird that we now think it’s even worse to disrespect money than it is to disrespect religion. Now, one of those contestants was Kate McGuinness. She poked fun at mining magnate Rinehart. I mean, what she said and did was not funny in any way, shape or form. I don’t have a great sense of humour myself. For example, I watch what passes for comedy and nothing ever happens. But I did run it past a few funsters in my life, and they didn’t think it was funny either.



But the reaction was out of control. Completely out of control. And that’s because Gina Rinehart has the entire right-wing media at her beck and call. She’s probs got Rupert allocated to the family chat. Aren’t we horrified that an overwhelmingly powerful, wealthy woman is bullying someone less than half her age? All hell broke loose, assisted by the hounds of Holt Street and the strays at Southbank. They’ve always hated the ABC, so this gave them even more fodder. Wonder why News Corp hates the national broadcaster? Always about money. The ABC gives away for free what News struggles to get people to pay for. ABC managing director Hugh Marks. Dominic Lorrimer Let’s get this out of the way. McGuinness’ comments about Rinehart weren’t any good. Silly. But the idea that she was trying to encourage violence is absolute rubbish. She’s a comedian trying to be funny. Good on her. With comedy as in life, it’s OK to fail and keep trying. Producers could have been more of a guiding hand, but I reckon the ABC is struggling with mentoring at the minute. I just don’t recall any of these folks getting particularly worked up about “ditch the witch”. It’s always OK to try to prick hugely inflated egos and status bubbles. We should always be about decapitating tall poppies. (Fortunately for me, at 149 centimetres and shrinking, I’ve only ever been a short poppy.)



What happened to the country I grew up in, joyfully poking fun at rich and powerful people? Are we now so frightened of status and influence that we don’t back the upstart? Sure, McGuinness wasn’t, ah, courteous, but why do we think that matters? Shall I give you a list of those who are neither tasteful nor polite? We would be here all day, because it would be a very long list. It is not the job of a comedian to be tasteful or polite. That is not the point. The point is to be funny and McGuinness will keep working on that so long as she isn’t bullied from her life’s work by Rinehart’s mates. If McGuinness could get to work on that racist member of the globalist elite, Pauline Hanson, that would be glorious. Related Article Exit Interview

Australian TV ‘Hate on my colleagues’: The brutal feedback Race Around the World contestants faced McGuinness is 29! (What I didn’t know at 29 would fill entire data centres). She’s on a very big stage, and she’s still on her L plates. Not tasteful? Geez, when I was her age, I made a three-part radio documentary on sex during menstruation, broadcast on community radio. Despite complaints to whatever ACMA was called back in the day, my station manager Keith Jackson, now retired in Noosa, backed me. And Hugh Marks? Glad he’s not my boss. What a suck-up to News Corp.



Just a reminder, Mr Marks. There are parts of News Corp that are promoting the globalist agenda of Pauline Hanson, the politician who won’t let the ABC into news conferences. Hanson, who is Rinehart’s buddy. Hanson, who is promoting the idea of defunding the ABC. Don’t cosy up to these people. It won’t work to protect you. What’s happening to Kate McGuinness is a pile-on and the ABC has folded like a concertina fan. The National Portrait Gallery had more gonads when it refused to buckle to Rinehart’s pressure to remove her portraits by Western Aranda artist Vincent Namatjira. The job of our cultural institutions is not to accept the billionaire view of the world, where might and money are always right. I asked Matthew Ricketson, co-author with Andrew Dodd of Getting Murdoched: How Murdoch’s Media Wields Power and Punishment*, now being reprinted, what he thought of the attacks on McGuinness. He described it as a classic News pile-on. Free speech is fine until you don’t agree with it. “Whatever the original offence was is far outweighed by the pile-on,” he said. “This is part of a sustained campaign to kick the ABC in the head.” Rinehart is doing her utmost to destroy McGuinness because the zillionaire’s feelings are hurt. She’s not a politician, but she’s trying to back one. We should all resist her and everyone who stands with her. And right now, that includes Hugh Marks.



* I’ve been a target of News and was interviewed for Getting Murdoched. Hey, Kate, trust me. You will survive. Jenna Price is a regular columnist.

World.title: It’s not just Gina Rinehart who failed to make a killing on SpaceX
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesElon Musk Opinion It’s not just Gina Rinehart who failed to make a killing on SpaceX Elizabeth Knight Business columnist August 11, 2026 — 3:32pm

August 11, 2026 — 3:32pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There are more than 28,000 Australian retail shareholders nursing a SpaceX sentiment sag – albeit they are in good company alongside our country’s richest person, Gina Rinehart. After Australia’s retail investors were given special permission (via prospectus additions) to buy directly into this blockbuster US float of Elon Musk’s rocket business in June, it was an irresistible punt for a cohort well known for their love of betting. For Rinehart, investing $1.4 billion of her fortune into SpaceX reflected her well-established Musk fan-girl credentials. It’s a big number, even if she can afford to lose some of it. But for the other 28,000-plus Australian mum and dad punters, there hasn’t been much joy or excitement in the financial return on their investment. The SpaceX IPO had a huge take-up of retail investors which made Elon Musk the world’s first trillionaire. Getty Images



After being the most hyped float of all time, the shares have spent half their public market life below the issue price. The only big winners were those that sold in the first week. This week the SpaceX share price has picked up a bit and now sits close to its issue price of $US135 ($191), so owners of the stock are no longer wearing an uncomfortable loss. It’s certainly better than last week’s low of $US104.83. But the buzz around this company was so noisy that retail investors were looking for a big payday. Retail investors didn’t punt on SpaceX just to get their money back. Last Friday marked a pivot point in trading when retail investors globally turned from net buyers to net sellers, according to tracking data from Vanda Research. There could be many reasons for this but reassessing the reward against the risk would be one.



Related Article Opinion

Sharemarket Burning billions: SpaceX’s sales are soaring, but its spending even more so Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Vanda estimates that retail traders on average paid $US147 for SpaceX shares since the initial public offering. It also cites evidence that retail investors had been actively buying the stock when it dipped. This average retail buy-in price is well below the current price, so the many sellers are simply cutting their losses. SpaceX is the ultimate casino-type bet. There are experts ascribing a value for SpaceX shares of $US800 and others who say it’s worth no more than $US100.



In only two months since its listing, the shares have moved between $US225 and $US104 – with little company news being reported, other than last week’s earnings report. The good news is that the company reported revenue that was generally higher than analysts were expecting, and management’s revenue forecasts were bullish. This should have provided some comfort to retail investors that underneath all that hot-air hype, the actual business was making decent strides. Gina Rinehart, a SpaceX investor, has praised the business and its founder Elon Musk. The bad news is that nothing in those performance numbers would support the nosebleed share prices at which SpaceX traded in the first couple of weeks after its float. In addition, the high proportion of big investors betting the stock price will fall (as much as one-third of the stock on issue has been sold “short”) is a headwind to share-price performance.



The release last week of almost 1 billion shares (held by staff and early investors) meant more SpaceX shares were added to the tally of those eligible to trade. That (over)supply shock was absorbed relatively well but it is the first of several releases of stock. Related Article Opinion

Sharemarket Is SpaceX a meme stock? Elon Musk loses trillionaire status Kishor Napier-Raman Senior Business Writer Each of the additions to the supply of stock will curb the scarcity value that helped push shares into the stratosphere in the first week following its debut. Now that the three-ring circus of the SpaceX listing has packed up, all investors will need to adjust to the reality that SpaceX shares will move in tandem with the market’s moveable appetite for risk. When US President Donald Trump’s war rhetoric towards Iran is toned down, or when the Federal Reserve makes dovish comments on US interest rates, SpaceX shares (and plenty of other risky shares) will respond positively.



But at moments when investors succumb to a bout of AI fear, SpaceX shares will catch a bout of that negative sentiment. Investors will also be watching whether management’s optimistic near-term revenue targets will be reached, rather than tracking Musk’s ambitions for earthlings to populate Mars.
