World.title: 230 in one boat: Migrants are piling onto mega-dinghies to get to UK
World.content:
WorldEuropeRefugees 230 in one boat: Migrants are piling onto mega-dinghies to get to UK Nick Gutteridge , Max Stephens , Vivian Song and Charles Hymas August 11, 2026 — 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

France’s lifeboat service has warned there is “no limit” to the number of migrants people-smugglers will put on a boat to Britain. The French national sea rescue service (SNSM) warned it was seeing “more and more” large boats ferrying hundreds of migrants across the Channel. A ‘mega-dinghy’ in action ferrying refugees across the English Channel from France. SNSM On Monday morning (UK time) a record 230 asylum seekers arrived in Britain after travelling on a single 15-metre-long vessel from near Berck-sur-Mer, Normandy. The vessel, which was intercepted by Border Force, HM Coastguard and the Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI), surpassed the previous record of 165 migrants who reached the UK in a single boat in July.



Jean-Marc Lamblin, the director of the SNSM’s Berck-sur-Mer branch, said: “Over the past three months we’ve been seeing more and more 15-metre boats passing through.” He added that when the 150-migrants-per-boat figure was recently surpassed, “we didn’t think there could be any more, but there really is no limit now”. Many of the “mega-dinghies” used for Channel crossings are manufactured in China, then shipped via commercial routes through countries such as Turkey and Bulgaria to European staging posts, chiefly Germany. International smuggling networks store and distribute them at the staging posts before they reach the French beaches from where they are launched. Home Office officials have previously identified Chinese websites as a key source of boats and parts, and have been working with Beijing to clamp down on them. A source at the National Crime Agency said China was “likely to be one of the countries but not the only country” from which smuggling gangs obtained their equipment.



Related Article Analysis

Immigration How the storming of Ceuta shifts Europe to the right It was not clear whether the mega-dinghy used in Monday’s crossing came from China. UK government sources said smuggling gangs were turning to such large vessels out of desperation to make the crossings financially viable. Last week people-smugglers packed 173 people onto a boat attempting to cross the Channel but they were returned to France after its engine caught fire. Joint operations between the British and French police on the ground have meant more planned launches are thwarted early, while co-operation with countries including Germany and China has helped restrict their supply of boats and engines.



French police are deploying new tactics to counter the growing use of mega-dinghies, including targeting and dispersing large gatherings of migrants near the coast, which are often a sign that a launch is imminent. As a result, the gangs were finding it increasingly difficult to launch enough small boats to make ends meet, officials said, meaning they were having to turn to cramming large numbers of migrants onto single-vessel voyages instead. Many of the “mega-dinghies” used for Channel crossings are manufactured in China and then shipped to European staging posts, chiefly Germany. SNSM A government source told The Telegraph: “Sustained pressure from law enforcement means the gangs are finding it harder to launch boats, and are therefore being forced to place more people onto them. “While this boat is larger, the number of crossings is down significantly, and we just had the lowest figures for a July since 2020.”



Officials said overall numbers of migrants arriving were down by 43 per cent compared with the previous year. This was despite the fact that August is one of the busiest periods of the year for “red days”, when sea conditions are most suitable for crossing. The average number of migrants per small boat has increased from seven in 2018 to 63 in the year to March, and 70 so far this month. But they warned that the smugglers’ use of larger boats had made both the crossings and the rescue operations at sea more perilous. The SNSM said about 30 people had ended up in the sea during the rush to climb on the mega-dinghy at about 5pm on Sunday. Some became cut off by the tide and needed to be rescued. French lifeboat workers noted that the large dinghy was first seen with about 50 migrants on board, then cruised close to a beach, picking up more people. The crowded dinghy was described as “buckling under the swell” as it headed towards Britain.



Dr Mihnea Cuibus, senior researcher at the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford, said: “There has been a longstanding trend of smugglers fitting increasingly more migrants onto larger and more crowded boats. “It is likely that this is at least partly driven by increased enforcement in and around the French coast. Related Article Immigration ‘Impenetrable border’: Farage claims Australian plan can stop the boats to Britain “Authorities have been trying to make it harder for smugglers to obtain boats, disrupting supply chains and confiscating equipment alongside European partners and thus creating incentives to fit as many people as possible into available boats.” The average number of migrants per small boat has increased from seven in 2018 to 63 in the year to March, and 70 so far this month.



Nigel Farage, the leader of Reform UK, said the record-breaking crossing proved the “illegal invasion is a national security emergency”. In a post on X he said: “At 2.30am this morning, a boat carrying 230 people was taken into Dover. This is a record number in a single vessel. It’s yet more proof that this illegal invasion is a national security emergency.” The boats are getting bigger as smuggling gangs look to make the crossings financially viable. Getty Images Chris Philp, the shadow home secretary, said the French authorities should have stopped the dinghy. He said: “This is now beyond a joke. The French authorities could easily have stopped a vessel this size from embarking in shallow waters. “I recently saw for myself French gendarmes standing by and doing nothing while illegal immigrants boarded in knee-deep water. Shabana Mahmood is handing over £660 million of our money while this happens. It’s a disgrace.”



Related Article Immigration People in this city want the boats to stop. But they haven’t met Rishan A spokesman for Europol, the EU’s law enforcement agency, said: “The European Centre Against Migrant Smuggling is aware of this development. “We are in constant exchange with the appropriate authorities in both France and the United Kingdom on this phenomenon and also have a dedicated operational taskforce running that concentrates on smuggling of migrants with boats (no matter if relatively small boats or, as of recently, larger boats) across the Channel.” A Home Office spokesman said: “This latest incident demonstrates the reckless and dangerous tactics employed by the criminal gangs facilitating these crossings, who continue to put lives at risk by cramming ever greater numbers of people onto unseaworthy vessels. “We are making progress, with the number of small boat crossings down this year and the lowest number recorded for the month of July since 2020.



“But we must go further, which is why we have signed a payment-by-results deal with the French to put 40 per cent more boots on the ground on French beaches.” The Telegraph, London Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Christopher Luxon refuses to speak to media as he arrives in Wellington ahead of urgent leadership meeting
World.content:
The Prime Minister Christopher Luxon refused to speak to reporters as he made his way through Wellington Airport ahead of an urgent caucus meeting on Wednesday.

His grip on National's leadership has come under scrutiny again after a series of missteps and clashes with coalition partners, including calling for an MMP referendum.

Caucus rumblings of rolling Luxon resurfaced in reporting by the New Zealand Herald on Monday evening, and by Tuesday afternoon Luxon had decided to call the urgent in-person meeting for Wednesday morning.

Former National MP on Luxon leadership speculation Checkpoint Download MP3 8m

"It is my firm belief that division and disunity are a major distraction only 90 days out from the election," he wrote.

The issue needed to be resolved quickly, he said.

Stepping off the plane in Wellington on Tuesday afternoon, Luxon told reporters, "talk to you tomorrow ... take care team".

National MPs were mostly keeping quiet on the matter, and had cleared their diaries on Wednesday morning - including the party's deputy Nicola Willis and third-ranked MP Chris Bishop both cancelling interview slots scheduled with RNZ's Morning Report.

Bishop, who is often tipped as a leadership contender, had two scheduled media events on Tuesday and faced questions about Luxon at both.

National's Chris Bishop. (File photo) RNZ / Mark Papalii

He threw his full support behind his leader and warned colleagues against leaking to media.

Asked again about the leadership at the second event, Bishop told reporters there was no update.

"Mate, we were just down the road in South Auckland 90 minutes ago," he said.

He then gave a running commentary about what had happened in those 90 minutes, including getting a coffee, preparing for his next speech and calling his wife.

Auckland Mayor Wayne Brown was with Bishop at the second event, standing beside him as they both took questions. Brown was asked if he wanted Bishop to be Prime Minister.

"Now there's a tricky question," Brown responded, chuckling.

Brown said Bishop was a "good bloke" but had a bit of competition for the National leadership, including from Defence Minister Chris Penk.

Penk had also been at the event, but did not stick around for the standup.

Brown said what he would really like was for the New Zealand public to choose the prime minister "instead of Winston Peters doing it."

National's James Meager told RNZ said he "absolutely" had confidence in Luxon.

"The media can interview themselves all they like about that, but its not anything we're interested in."

Meager suggested not trusting everything in the media, and referenced being quoted in the Herald in November "making claims about things about me that were entirely untrue, which have been repeated throughout the media despite the fact them not being true."

It had been reported that Meager was canvassing support for Bishop to take over as leader.

"It's false, and I denied it," Meager said.

"I'm not really interested in people's views on speculation about any of that sort of stuff, because as far as I'm concerned, it's nonsense."

He said he'd had no conversations with his fellow MPs about a change in leadership in recent days.

Senior MP Todd McClay also said he was behind Luxon.

"He's doing a good job, he's an excellent Prime Minister, he has my one hundred percent support."

National MPs front media at Wellington Airport

Arriving at Wellington Airport on Tuesday afternoon, National MP Scott Simpson told reporters he "absolutely" had confidence in the Prime Minister.

He would not speculate about whether a confidence vote would be held during Wednesday's meeting.

"I've never talked about caucus matters until now, and I'm not going to start today."

Southland MP Joseph Mooney said he supported his leader, and no other contenders had requested his backing.

"Any discussions will be in that caucus room, if there are any discussions to be had," he said.

"I don't have any reason to think there's gonna be a call for a vote tomorrow."

Mooney said Luxon had himself acknowledged the "challenges" he'd faced in the past week.

"That is what it is."

Hawke's Bay-based MPs Katie Nimon and Catherine Wedd also said they "absolutely" had confidence in Luxon.

"We are just happy to get back to our electorates, as fast as possible, get back to the mighty Hawke's Bay and focus on the people of Hawke's Bay ... and the things that matter," Wedd said.

"That's right," said Nimon.

Wedd would not confirm whether she would give Luxon her vote if one was held.

"We don't talk about what happens in caucus... we're 100 percent behind the Prime Minister, and we're 100 percent behind our caucus leadership."

Meanwhile Labour's deputy leader Carmel Sepuloni wouldn't speculate but said: "clearly they're not performing very well and there's unrest in the National party caucus - hence why they're meeting."

Sepuloni said disunity or ruptures in the National party caucus was not an issue for Labour.

World.title: Water should be flowing again in Ohakune
World.content:
Residents in the central North Island town of Ohakune should be seeing water reappear in their taps again.

The supply's been without water since Sunday as a break in the town's main pipeline, caused by an earthquake last month, was repaired.

A boil water notice was in place as a precaution, while authorities test to see if the supply is safe to drink.

It was originally expected the water network would return to normal on Monday evening, but that was pushed out by 24 hours. The outage has caused schools and eateries in the town to close, and the Ruapehu District Council has provided a water tank, containers of water and portaloos for the town's 1400 residents.

Colin Young fills a water bottle. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

Ruapehu Civil Defence controller Vini Dutra thanked Ohakune residents for their patience during the outage.

"Please continue to use water sparingly over the coming days so the reservoir can fully recover and pressure can be restored to normal levels," he said.

The council has asked residents to turn on outside taps and let them flow to help clear air from the pipes, while their inside ones were kept off.

"Taps may splutter when first turned on. This is just trapped air being released and is nothing to worry about," the council said.

"Water may also look milky. This is caused by air bubbles and is not a health concern. Low pressure may continue to be noticed until the reservoir has refilled several times."

What happened

The council's water services are contracted to Veolia.

A company spokesperson said on Tuesday afternoon the network was being flushed to make sure drinking water would be available as quickly as possible.

"The crack in the pipe caused by the earthquake remained undetected because no system data indicated a major leak," the spokesperson said.

"The leak was only discovered in dense bushland by a passing bush walker.

"Veolia took this seriously and responded immediately, as soon as it became aware of the crack, as this critical piece of infrastructure supplies water to the Ohakune Reservoir and is the town's only water supply," they said.

"If there had been a complete break it would have been far worse, with longer impacts."

Veolia worked quickly to repair the pipeline, in what it said was a hard-to-access area, and brought in extra staff from throughout New Zealand.

"The pipe was repaired quickly, but it is much more complex restarting the flow in a 7 kilometre-long, gravity-fed pipeline than simply switching on a garden hose.

"Air can become trapped if the water is simply switched back on at full capacity, which could cause pressure to build up and potentially lead to multiple breakages along its length."

The spokesperson said that air had to be cleared and the pipeline reopened in sections.

They thanked the community and said once the outage was resolved it would do a review of what happened and its processes.

On Tuesday, the council said it was too soon to answer questions about whether it could seek to fine or take other action against Veolia because of the outage, or whether closed businesses could get financial assistance.

"Far too early to answer that - we are still in response mode," a spokesman said.

"When the water is safely back on there will be a review of what happened ... and those issues will be looked at then."

A water truck in Ohakune supplying drinking water. RNZ / Kate Pereyra

School stays shut, businesses scramble

Ruapehu College stayed closed on Tuesday.

Principal Kris Vine said staff were staying in touch with the school's 250 students.

He was waiting on more information so he could plan the school's reopening, and communicate information to students' families.

"Most students are probably not too disappointed with not coming to school, to a certain extent, but I know that they'll be missing their mates and, obviously, there's the realisation of what water means to a community," he said.

"It's probably a nice little learning curve and a timely reminder about emergency planning and that kind of stuff for whānau that are dealing with it."

Students from places such as Waimarino or Raetihi weren't affected by the outage.

"I'm just here waiting for phone calls and checking in on any updates and things," Vine said.

"It's a nice little admin day, so to speak, but also a bit of a sit-and-wait kind of day, which is long."

At The Peaks Motor Inn, manager Remi Butler previously told RNZ the motel had taken a financial hit when a large group booking cancelled.

After the council confirmed the water would be out until Tuesday evening, she said she was disappointed and stressed by the news.

She said she and her husband were even contemplating buying a pump to get river water to flush toilets at the motel.

World.title: Pauline Hanna inquest: Philip Polkinghorne accused of 'pretending' during some of 111 call
World.content:
Philip Polkinghorne has been accused "pretending" over some of the actions he said he took the morning he found his wife dead in their home.

He denies the claim by police counsel Alysha McClintock at an inquest into the 2021 death of his wife Pauline Hanna.

Polkinghorne was acquitted of her murder in 2024.

He became irritated several times under cross examination by McClintock.

McClintock honed in on actions Polkinghorne said he has taken when he stepped away from a 111 call for 10 seconds.

The details of those actions are suppressed.

She accused Polkinghorne of "pretending" to do what he said he had done because the timing meant it was not possible.

Polkinghorne disagreed, saying sarcastically he should have videoed the whole event.

That prompted Coroner Tania Tehitaha to intervene, asking him not to use sarcasm.

Polkinghorne appeared frustrated when McClintock persisted with her timing theory.

"There is no evidence for whatever your ridiculous postulate is which you keep harping on about," he said.

McClintock noted Polkinghorne's evidence had changed several times since he was first interviewed by police.

He agreed and also agreed that some of what he was telling the coroner at the hearing was different to previous evidence.

But that could be explained by his distress and shock when he was first interviewed, he said.

World.title: Schools ban Ooshies after fights, distractions and some going missing
World.content: On social media, Māngere central School said Ooshies had become a significant distraction during class time and break time. It and said due to the high demand there had been situations where they had gone missing or been misplaced, which led to upset students and lost learning time.

World.title: The South Island's 10 plans for reshaping local government
World.content:
Big changes to the country's council boundaries are in the government's hands, now that the deadline has passed for councils to state their preferences.

Ten different reorganisation models have been proposed by 27 South Island councils, including a vast new unitary authority spanning the central and eastern parts of the Mainland and two conflicting models for Southland.

In May, councils were given three months to come up with proposals to create larger and more efficient unitary councils or have the government do it for them.

Government officials will assess the Head Start proposals and decide by the end of September if they are realistic and deliver better value to ratepayers.

Local Government Minister Simon Watts told Morning Report on Tuesday that he was impressed by the number of proposals put forward.

"This is going to form a more efficient local government system that's more fit for purpose. We know the current model is too complex and [has] too much duplication," he said.

Approved plans will be signed off in 2027, with changes expected to take effect from the 2028 local elections.

Nelson and Tasman: no proposal

As unitary councils, Nelson City Council and Tasman District Council were not explicitly included in the Head Start process.

Nelson was still exploring a merger but Tasman was not interested.

Nelson mayor Nick Smith wrote on Facebook he was disappointed the councils had not grasped an opportunity for change.

"Nelson and Tasman are one interdependent economy - we sink or swim together. The duplicate bureaucracy of having two councils adds extra costs for ratepayers," he said.

Tasman mayor Tim King told RNZ the councils already collectively owned a significant amount of infrastructure and assets.

"We work very closely and there's heaps of scope to do more of that. My perspective is that the last thing you give up in any democratic system is your vote or your representation," he said.

You exhaust every other opportunity to make the efficiencies or cost savings before you give up your vote and your representation."

Marlborough and Kaikōura: merger

In one of the simpler amalgamation proposals, Marlborough District Council and Kaikōura District Council agreed to form a partnership and create an extended unitary authority from 2028.

Their joint Head Start proposal sets out plans to maintain a "strong local voice for Kaikōura" by establishing a Kaikōura ward with three dedicated Kaikōura-based councillors.

The councils said they had a shared tourism economy, transport corridors and coastal and marine interests.

The partnership would allow both districts to diversify their economies, attract investment and reduce their reliance on any single sector, they said.

"The merger is not without risk. While Marlborough District Council is experienced in managing regional council functions, it does not have the same scale or number of ratepayers as the Canterbury region has to address the impacts of storm events," the councils said.

West Coast: merger

Grey and Westland district councils submitted a proposal for a joint unitary authority encompassing all of the West Coast, despite a split vote from Buller District Council which did not endorse the plan.

"The proposal nevertheless remains eligible for submission under the government's Head Start criteria, which require support from a majority of the directly affected territorial authorities," the councils said.

They said the proposal was not a decision to establish a new council, rather examining whether the model would work.

Westland mayor Helen Lash said any changes should be informed by independent evidence, meaningful community input and a clear understanding of the long-term benefits and challenges.

North Canterbury: merger

Waimakariri and Hurunui district councils have teamed up on a proposal to create a new North Canterbury council.

They said the model would let the districts build on long-standing collaboration, rather than creating entirely new governance arrangements.

Hurunui mayor Marie Black said the move would keep North Canterbury's future in the region's hands.

"North Canterbury already functions as a connected community. Our residents work together, support one another through challenges, share services and infrastructure and increasingly see themselves as part of a wider North Canterbury story," she said.

Selwyn: standalone council

Selwyn District Council was seeking to establish a standalone Selwyn Unitary Authority, absorbing regional council functions within its existing boundaries.

Selwyn mayor Lydia Gliddon said it was the preferred option among a survey of ratepayers.

"Our community has told us they value strong local representation, local decision-making and a future that keeps Selwyn's priorities at the forefront," she said.

Christchurch: standalone council

Similarly, Christchurch City Council agreed to keep its current city boundaries and absorb regional council functions to create a new unitary authority.

Mayor Phil Mauger wanted a greater Christchurch metropolitan option that included Rangiora, Rolleston and other towns but failed to gain majority support.

He said he would not lose sleep over the "missed opportunity".

"The council made the decision and we're head down and get on with it," he said.

Mid-South Canterbury/North Otago: merger

Timaru, Mackenzie, Waimate and Waitaki district councils jointly lodged what they described as a bold and ambitious proposal for a vast new unitary authority spanning the central and eastern South Island.

Their proposal also assumed the inclusion of Ashburton District, despite Ashburton councillors equally split between four reform options and deciding not to submit a proposal.

The councils said their 26,900 square kilometre patch from the Rakaia River in the north to the Waitaki River in the south was one of the country's most productive and strategically important regions.

"Local government remains divided across multiple councils and two regional jurisdictions. This proposal is about correcting that mismatch and better leveraging its resources and talents to drive success locally, regionally and nationally," they said.

Central Otago & Clutha: merger

Central Otago and Clutha district councils were earlier working with Queenstown Lakes on a proposal for a single, provincial council capturing their "mountains to the sea" region.

Queenstown Lakes then decided to walk away in pursuit of a partnership with Dunedin City Council.

Central Otago and Clutha district councils said they were disappointed but the proposal would still go to government.

Clutha mayor Jock Martin said the proposal was well thought out and had merit.

Inland and Coastal Otago: twin model

Queenstown Lakes District Council agreed to work with Dunedin City Council on a twin model for Otago, consisting of an Inland Otago Unitary Authority and a Coastal Otago Unitary Authority.

Queenstown mayor John Glover said the proposal would give the district a seat at the table and time for more detailed exploration of a potential governance model.

"It does not represent a final decision on any future council structure. It simply allows us to positively contribute to the conversation," he said.

Southland: merger or twin model

Southland councils have submitted two conflicting proposals that include Gore.

The first submitted by Invercargill City Council would see all four existing local authorities - Invercargill, Southland, Gore and Southland Regional Council - replaced with a single, region-wide unitary council.

Mayor Tom Campbell said the proposal was about creating "a governance model that reflects how Southland already works" while ensuring a strong voice for rural and urban communities.

The second submitted by Southland District Council would see it team up with Gore District Council to form a new rural unitary authority, while Invercargill city would remain a separate unitary authority.

Southland mayor Rob Scott said the twin model reflected community feedback and had the backing of Federated Farmers Southland.

"Our focus is on ensuring Southland communities are represented in shaping their own future," he said.

"The Head Start process has been rushed and we would have liked to have more time to talk to our people and the other councils in Southland but we believe it is important to be part of this to ensure the best outcome for our region."

Gore District Council has given its support to both proposals.

Mayor Ben Bell said he wanted to keep the district at the table, rather than committing to any particular model.

World.title: The Luxon dilemma: Should he stay or should he go?
World.content:
Analysis: Christopher Luxon's leadership is hanging by a thread as he arrives in Wellington ready to face his opponents in caucus on Wednesday morning.

In April he stared down his agitators and called a vote of confidence in himself to prove he still had a mandate as National Party leader.

He succeeded in that vote but at the same time put an extraordinary amount of pressure on himself to personally perform better and lift his polling.

There was no chance the caucus leaking and destabilisation would stop unless that happened, and on both measures Luxon has fallen short.

On the latter, the party's polling remains woefully low - last month National was down 2.1 points in the RNZ-Reid Research poll to 28.7 percent.

It was the party's fourth consecutive decline in the Reid Research series and its weakest result since Luxon became leader in November 2021.

On the former, Luxon's personal performance has had moments of reprieve from gaffes and the occasional show of strength but that was all undone last week - a week now dubbed his worst in his prime ministership.

From apologies to business leaders and defending using an NZDF plane to fly him home after a National Party fundraiser, to an 11-year unemployment high, a call to hold a referendum on MMP blindsiding his colleagues in the process, and then a political attack on Labour that derailed into three new National taxes, Luxon went from one disaster to the next.

When Luxon fronted media in April having secured a win in that confidence vote he single-handedly blamed "speculation and rumour" and a "media soap opera" for the position he'd found himself in.

There was no self-reflection that perhaps he hadn't done enough to keep his caucus happy, listened to their concerns, taken onboard their advice, or been willing to change to try lift the party's chances ahead of the November election.

Instead he sent a message direct to the destabilisation faction of the caucus that they were to blame and he had beaten them.

When the rumoured result of that confidence vote started circling in the past week it was clear the anti-Luxon faction were saddling the horses and getting ready to go.

It's now been widely reported that vote was 27-22 and when it was put to Luxon on Saturday he didn't deny it, instead saying he had the support of his caucus.

In theory Luxon doesn't know the result, only party president Sylvia Wood and junior whip Suze Redmayne who did the count know the number, but it's possible MPs dissatisfied with Luxon have been calling around their colleagues and firming up a rough idea of where the vote landed at the time.

If it's true then it would only take three MPs flipping their vote for Luxon to be goneburger.

In the past two weeks Luxon has made two captain calls without first consulting his caucus.

The first was ruling out any arrangement with Opportunity after the election if National is in a position to govern, and the second on Thursday was a commitment to hold a referendum on the MMP voting system.

Captain's calls aren't uncommon but they are usually done from a position of strength and power by a leader who enjoys wide support from their caucus.

Both Sir John Key and Dame Jacinda Ardern made them and did so successfully. Luxon is not Key or Ardern.

If Luxon can't keep his caucus on side - something he'll already know the answer to by the time he heads into that do-or-die meeting - he'll either have to step aside to make way for a new leader or be pushed by his colleagues.

Luxon and any supporters he still has will be hitting the phones late into the evening getting an indication of whether he still has a majority backing him, and if he can win a vote if he calls one.

But that's only half of the issue.

A confidence vote was won four months ago and the prime minister was adamant it had put the matter to bed and here he is again reliving the worst 24 hours of his political career to date.

Winning a confidence vote and trying to keep his caucus in line between now and November 7 could prove more difficult than facing the reality he's no longer the man for the job.

There are just six weeks until the House rises and the official six-week campaign kicks off, and at this point the National Party billboards could be emblazoned with the face of Luxon, Nicola Willis, Erica Stanford, Chris Bishop, or some other outside chance from the front bench.

When Luxon posted on social media that he had called his caucus to Wellington he said it was his "firm belief that division and disunity are a major distraction only 90 days out from the election".

World.title: Wellington Hospital ED has busiest day in almost a year
World.content:
Wellington Hospital's Emergency Department had its busiest day for almost a year on Monday, seeing a total of 258 patients.

Health NZ said this compared with an average of 189 a day last month.

But it added as a caveat that the data was operational and was subject to change following a a quality assurance process.

The agency said there had been high demand over the last few days and some staff sickness.

Robert Blaikie, interim deputy group director of operations, said winter was a busy time for healthcare providers.

"Despite these pressures, our dedicated staff continued to provide safe, compassionate and professional care in extremely difficult circumstances. I would like to thank them for their dedication and professionalism."

He said staff had increased temporary capacity and frequently reviewed patients to see if they might be discharged sooner.

He said preparations for winter had been underway since March, including more staff, beds and community care.

The capital's urgent care clinic's opening hours are being extended to give patients alternative options.

A specialised elderly care nurse will support earlier discharge for senior patients in the Hutt Valley.

A nurse will be introduced to a pharmacy in Porirua and four in the Hutt Valley.

Health NZ advised the public to get their flu and whooping cough jabs to protect themsleves and the wider community.

World.title: Vaping emerges as a risk for infant deaths
World.content:
Vaping while pregnant - or even while sharing a bed with a baby - is emerging as a risk for death in infants.

A University of Auckland study has found vaping is showing similar risks as smoking, particularly when combined with sharing a bed with an infant.

Professor Ed Mitchell said vaping had been widely regarded as safer than smoking, even while pregnant or sharing a bed with an infant.

But the study "raises the possibility that the effects of nicotine itself, rather than how nicotine is delivered, may be contributing to infant vulnerability".

Research found smoking or vaping was reported in nearly three quarters of a series of infant deaths from 2022 and 2023.

Out of 66 sudden infant deaths studied, close to 70 percent were sharing a bed with a parent who smoked or vaped.

Mitchell said the findings raised a fundamental question about current pregnancy advice.

"Vaping has been widely approached as a safer alternative to smoking and a smoking cessation aid, including in pregnancy. Our findings suggest we need to consider all nicotine exposure during pregnancy, particularly when it is combined with bed sharing."

He said when the consequence could be death, precautions should be taken.

Researchers called for public health messaging around vaping during pregnancy to be reassessed.

Several experts supported the study's findings and precautionary approach.

Dr Gergely Toldi from Starship Newborn Services said the increasing proportions of Māori and Pacific infants affected call for urgent, culturally appropriate communication of health advice and safety netting for whānau.

"I welcome the suggestion that complete nicotine cessation should be encouraged in NZ during pregnancy, breastfeeding and in households with a small pēpi less than one year of age instead of recommending vaping as an acceptable alternative," Toldi said.

Research associate professor Andrew Waa said government policies were needed to protect families from using cigarettes and vapes, rather than making them more available.

"Traditionally we have had success supporting mothers to quit smoking while pregnant but relapse after birth has always been a challenge, particularly if other family members continue to smoke."

Waa said the study showed that we must be precautionary and protect babies from exposure to nicotine.

Plunket's chief nurse Dr Zoe Tipa said the findings of the study reinforce Plunket's existing advice that nay nicotine-free environment is the safest during pregnancy, and for babies to sleep in.

She said she hoped the findings wouldn't create fear, guilt or whakamā among whānau .

"We want whānau to know what they can do now, and where they can find support, any small steps they can take to being nicotine-free are positive steps," she said.

Tipa encouraged whānau to speak to health professionals they trusted, to get a plan for supporting them reach their goals.

The Ministry of Health's director of public health Dr Corina Grey said they welcomed the study's contribution to the understanding of potential risk factors for SUDI.

"Our advice to everyone remains that is it best to be smokefree and vape-free, including during pregnancy or when caring for young babies. Babies are safest when they are in an environment that is smoke-free, vape-free, alcohol-free, and drug-free.

"While there is clear and well-established evidence that smoking harms babies' health and increases the risk of SUDI, the evidence for vaping is not clear and well established.

"Vaping is less harmful than smoking and vaping remains an effective cessation tool. However, where possible, we strongly encourage people not to vape when pregnant, or around children and babies," she said.

Grey said the ministry continued to monitor emerging evidence about potential harms from vaping, including on children and babies.

When asked for thoughts on the study's findings, Health Minister Simeon Brown's office said vaping and maternal health sat with the Associate Health Minister Casey Costello.

World.title: 'Never forgotten where he's from': Outback community pride for Crows legend
World.content:
Taylor Walker will go down in history as an AFL legend but when all is said and done, the boy from the bush wants to return home and attempt to win a premiership in the town that made him.

Walker announced his retirement from the Adelaide Crows Football Club on Monday after 19 seasons playing for the AFL club.

The 36-year-old's playing career started in the outback New South Wales community of Broken Hill, located just over the South Australian border.

"I've said to my two best mates that are still playing back in Broken Hill that I want to go and try and win a premiership back there, so we'll try and do that next year," he said in his retirement announcement speech.

Jayden Kelly is one of those mates and says he is holding Walker to that promise.

Jayden Kelly played junior footy with Walker, and is hopeful he'll come back to Broken Hill and play. (ABC News: Bill Ormonde)

"He has mentioned it once or twice that he would love to [come back]. So there's myself and a couple of his close mates that are just hanging on and still playing local footy back here," he said.

Walker is no stranger to a winning a flag with the North Broken Hill Football Club.

As a self-proclaimed "skinny kid from Broken Hill", the then 17-year-old helped the Bulldogs to premiership glory in 2007.

Taylor Walker (left) was instrumental in the 2007 grand final, when the North Broken Hill Bulldogs won. (Supplied: Gavin Schmidt)

Broken Hill inspiration

But while Taylor Walker will undoubtably be remembered for his on-field contributions for the Crows, the legacy he leaves in Broken Hill is just as significant.

Kelly said Walker's career had shown young people in the town what could be possible.

"He's really put us on the map," he said.

"He's shown young kids in Broken Hill, if they put their mind to it and by working hard, what they can achieve."

Kelly, who played junior football alongside Walker, said he remembered feeling it was "unreal" to see a boy from Broken Hill picked when he was drafted .

"Being able to go and live out a childhood dream; he supported the crows growing up and had all the Tony Modra posters all over his wall," he said.

"He loved everything Crows and when he got the phone call that they were interested ... he was over the moon."

Taylor Walker plays alongside fellow Crow and Broken Hill export Isaac Cumming. (Supplied: AFC Media)

Wayne Walker is Taylor Walker's dad who proudly remains living in the outback town.



He said he had most admired his son's relationship with his family, the Adelaide Crows and club supporters.

"He's always never forgotten where he come from. His mates are so dear to him, it's not funny, they keep him grounded," he said.

"That's probably one thing he has been, he's been very grounded during the whole 19 years."

Walker's friends and family say he's never forgotten where he came from. (Supplied: Gavin Schmidt)

It is a sentiment Walker's friend, Jayden Kelly agreed with.

"He's had so many ups and downs, the resilience he has shown, and he's never forgotten where he's come from," he said.

"He's so loyal to the people around him, to his family, and to the town that he grew up in.

World.title: Aussie open water swim queen Johnson triumphs at Pan Pacs
World.content:
Australia's world champion Moesha Johnson has continued her season of complete dominance in open water swimming, winning the Pan Pacific Championships 10-kilometre title off Long Beach, California.

Racing on the same waterfront expected to be used for the 2028 Olympics, 28-year-old Johnson grabbed the lead on the second of six laps and won comfortably in one hour 55 minutes and 33 seconds on Tuesday (AEST).

She finished more than 26 seconds clear of silver medallist Airi Ebina of Japan, with Ichika Kajimoto (Japan) third and fellow Australian Jacqueline Davison-McGovern fifth in the 23-strong field.

"I really wanted to win going into the race today, and it's a strong group of girls, they're really fit and everyone's in really good shape," Johnson said after the race.

"Realistically I had to keep an eye on where my heart rate and my effort was sitting and Jacqui (Davison-McGovern) was there at my feet the whole way.

"I wanted to keep her with me but at the end I just wanted to make sure I had the gears to keep shifting [up].

"I really wanted to have a dominating race on American soil leading into LA '28.

"Even when I was well ahead at the end I just wanted to keep putting on a show for everyone."

The victory extended a dazzling 2026 campaign for Johnson, who won all four World Cup 10km races plus all four 3km races.

The 2024 Olympic silver medallist is a three-time world championship gold medallist, having won 5km and 10km last year in Singapore.
